title: Design Uber (ride-hailing)
summary: Uber is a real-time two-sided marketplace: millions of drivers stream GPS every 4 seconds, riders expect a car offer in under 2 seconds, and every match must give one driver to exactly one rider while money moves with zero loss. The core tension is that dispatch wants availability and low latency (an AP, in-memory, geo-sharded system where a slightly stale location is fine) while trips and payments want correctness (a CP, durable, idempotent system where a duplicate charge or double-assigned driver is a headline). The design is really about drawing that boundary cleanly and keeping each side failing safely.

clarify: Scope: I will cover rider request -> match -> pickup -> trip -> payment -> rating end to end, with deepest focus on location ingestion, geo indexing and dispatch. UberEats, pooled rides and scheduled rides I treat as extensions unless you want them in.
Scale assumption: about 25M trips per day globally, 5M drivers online at peak, each pinging GPS every 4 s, which is roughly 1.25M location writes per second at peak.
Latency targets: driver offer within 2 s p95 of a request, nearby-cars map on the rider app refreshed every 3-5 s, live driver position on the rider's map within about 2 s of reality.
Consistency: a driver must never be assigned to two trips at once, and a rider must never be charged twice. Location data may be a few seconds stale; trip state and money may not.
Geography: is the market multi-region and multi-country? I will assume yes, with data residency rules in some countries (India, EU), so city -> region pinning matters.
Matching objective: nearest-driver by ETA, or global efficiency? I will start with greedy nearest-ETA and evolve to batched bipartite matching in dense cities.
Pricing: is surge in scope? I will assume yes, computed per hexagon per minute from streaming supply and demand, and locked into an upfront fare quote the rider accepts.
Payments: cards, wallets, UPI and cash; I will assume a PSP (Stripe/Adyen/Razorpay class) does card networking and we own the ledger, idempotency and auth/capture orchestration.
Mobile reality: drivers move through tunnels and 2G zones, so the client must be designed to survive network drops mid-trip and the server must tolerate out-of-order, late pings.
design: Baseline first: one region, a stateless API, Postgres with PostGIS, drivers POST location, dispatch runs a radius query and offers the closest driver. Works to a few thousand drivers and then the write rate and the radius query fall over.
Edge: rider and driver apps hold a persistent connection (WebSocket/MQTT-style over TLS) to a gateway fleet; requests carry an idempotency key; gateways rate-limit per user and device.

Location ingestion: driver pings go to a Location Service that writes the latest position into an in-memory geo index sharded by city and H3 cell (Ringpop-style consistent hashing), and appends the raw ping to Kafka for trails, ETA training and fraud.
Geo index: H3 resolution 8-9 cells as keys, each cell holding a set of available driver ids; nearby search = kRing around the rider's cell, filtered by vehicle type and state.

Dispatch (DISCO-style): Demand Service accepts a ride request with an upfront quote; Matcher takes candidates from the geo index, ranks them by road-network ETA, and either offers greedily or collects a 1-2 s batch and solves a bipartite assignment per city cell.

Driver lock: before an offer goes out the matcher atomically flips the driver from AVAILABLE to OFFERED with a lease (compare-and-set with a fencing token) so no second matcher can grab the same driver; the lease expires in about 15 s if the driver does not answer.

Trip Service owns the trip state machine (REQUESTED -> MATCHED -> ARRIVING -> ON_TRIP -> COMPLETED / CANCELLED) in a strongly consistent store (Docstore-like, Raft per partition), with every transition emitted to Kafka via an outbox.

Payments as a saga: authorize the estimated fare at request time, capture the final fare at completion, refund or void on cancel, every PSP call keyed by a deterministic idempotency key, double-entry ledger as the source of truth, reconciliation daily.
Pricing: a Flink job reads request and supply events from Kafka, aggregates per H3 cell per minute, smooths, and writes multipliers to a key-value store that the quote API reads in under 5 ms.
ETA: routing engine on a contraction-hierarchy road graph with live traffic weights, plus an ML residual model (DeepETA-style) that corrects the routing ETA from historical outcomes.
defend: Bottleneck one is the location write path (1.25M/s). It is absorbed by keeping only the latest position per driver in memory, sharding by geography, batching on the gateway, and sending the durable trail asynchronously through Kafka instead of a database write.

Scaling reads: nearby-car queries (hundreds of thousands per second) hit the same in-memory shards; we serve them from read replicas of each cell shard and coarsen them (cars shown on the map can be 5 s stale and snapped to a cell), so they never contend with dispatch.
Scaling writes for trips: trip rows are partitioned by trip_id hash inside each region's Docstore; one trip only ever has one leader, so state transitions serialize cheaply.
Hot spots: stadium exits and airports overload one cell; we split hot cells to a finer H3 resolution, give airports a dedicated FIFO queue service, and batch match there.

Failure of matching: the matcher is stateless over the geo index and driver leases; if a shard owner dies, SWIM detects it in a few seconds, Ringpop reassigns its cells, and drivers' next pings (within 4 s) rebuild the index. Requests in flight retry with jitter.

Region loss: cities are pinned to a home region with an active standby; state that must survive (trip, payment) is replicated; dispatch rebuilds from driver pings and from an encrypted trip digest stored on the driver phone, as Uber described doing.

Payments safety: CP store, idempotency keys on every hop, auth before match, capture after trip, compensating refund/void steps, and a ledger reconciliation job that alerts on any non-zero imbalance. We would rather delay a capture than double it.

Degradation ladder: under stress, drop nearby-cars refresh rate first, then fall back from batched to greedy matching, then use cached surge, then serve ETAs from haversine x city factor; never degrade the driver lock or the ledger.

What I measure: request-to-offer p95, offer acceptance rate, match rate, unfulfilled requests per cell, location ingest lag, ETA error (MAPE), double-assignment count (must be 0), payment capture success, ledger imbalance (must be 0), and websocket connected ratio.
framework.script: Let me clarify scope first. I will design the full ride flow, request to payment, but go deepest on location ingestion, geospatial indexing and dispatch, because that is where the scale is. I will assume 25 million trips a day and 5 million drivers online at peak, each sending GPS every 4 seconds, so about 1.25 million location writes per second. The hard requirements are an offer within 2 seconds, never assigning one driver to two riders, and never charging twice. Locations can be a few seconds stale; trips and money cannot. So my design splits into two worlds. The real-time world is in-memory and AP: drivers stream pings over a persistent connection, a location service keeps only the latest position in a geo index keyed by H3 hexagons and sharded by city with consistent hashing and gossip membership, and the matcher pulls candidates, ranks them by road ETA and locks one driver with a lease before sending the offer. The durable world is CP: the trip state machine lives in a Raft-replicated store, and payments are a saga of authorize then capture, with idempotency keys and a double-entry ledger. Kafka connects the two and feeds surge pricing in Flink. Then I will defend it: the write path, hot cells, the double-assignment race, region loss and what I would measure.

brd.problem: Riders in a city need a car within minutes at a predictable price, and drivers need a steady stream of nearby, worthwhile trips. Without a central marketplace, riders wait on street corners and drivers drive empty. The business must match supply and demand in real time, price to balance them, move money reliably between three parties (rider, driver, platform), and do it safely in hundreds of cities with different laws, networks and payment habits.
goals: Get a rider matched to a driver within seconds and picked up within the quoted ETA.
Maximise completed trips per hour per city (marketplace efficiency), not just individual nearest matches.
Keep driver utilisation high (less dead mileage between trips) so earnings per hour stay attractive and supply stays on the platform.
Price transparently with an upfront fare and use dynamic pricing to restore balance when demand outruns supply.
Move money correctly: every completed trip charged exactly once, every driver paid exactly what the ledger says, reconciled daily.
Stay available through datacenter and region loss, with no trip lost mid-ride.
Keep riders and drivers safe: verified identities, live trip sharing, SOS, fraud controls.
Comply per country: data residency, tax invoices, regulator reporting, licensed-driver checks.
non_goals: Building our own mapping company from scratch on day one; we license base maps and layer our own traffic and pickup-point data.
Acting as a card network or bank; a PSP handles card rails and settlement.
Perfect global optimality of every match; near-optimal within a 1-2 s window is the target.
Autonomous vehicle fleet management and freight logistics in this version.
Food delivery multi-stop batching (UberEats) beyond reusing the same platform pieces.

stakeholders.needs: Fast pickup, accurate ETA, fair and predictable price, safety.
Steady nearby trips, clear earnings, fast payouts, fair ratings, battery and data friendly app.
Levers for surge, incentives, airport queues and events; real-time city dashboards.
Accurate ledger, tax invoices, SOX controls, audit trails, regulator data feeds.
Fraud signals, GPS spoof detection, incident replay of trip trails.
Failover playbooks, observability, capacity headroom for New Year's Eve peaks.

success_metrics.metric: Match rate (requests that get a driver)
success_metrics.target: >= 95% in core cities outside extreme surge
median absolute error under 1 min; 90% within 2 min

constraints: Mobile clients on flaky 2G/3G/4G networks with GPS noise of 5-50 m, worse in urban canyons.
Driver phones are battery and data constrained, so ping rate is about 4 s, not 1 s.
Data residency: some countries require rider PII and trip data to stay in-country.
Payment rails differ per market: cards, wallets, UPI, cash; PSP latency 300 ms to 3 s.
Regulatory caps on surge in some cities and on driver working hours in others.
Peaks are spiky: New Year's Eve, concerts and rain can be 5-10x normal in minutes.

risks.risk: Double-assigning a driver during a network partition between matchers
risks.mitigation: Single owner per driver via consistent hashing plus a lease with fencing token in the driver-state store; offer only after CAS succeeds.

risks.risk: Duplicate or lost charges after retries and PSP timeouts
risks.mitigation: Deterministic idempotency keys, auth/capture split, ledger as source of truth, daily reconciliation with the PSP settlement file.
Replicated trip store, client-held trip digest, warm standby region per city, regular failover drills.

risks.risk: GPS spoofing and fake trips (driver-rider collusion for incentives)
risks.mitigation: Speed and teleport checks, device integrity, graph-based collusion detection, payout holds for anomalous earnings.

risks.risk: Surge pricing perceived as gouging during emergencies
risks.mitigation: Caps and emergency overrides per city, smoothing, transparent upfront fare, policy team controls.

risks.risk: Hot-cell overload at events breaks dispatch for the whole city shard
risks.mitigation: Cell splitting, bulkheaded queues per zone, airport/event FIFO queues, load shedding of non-critical reads first.

user_stories: As a rider, I want to see nearby cars and an ETA before I request so that I know whether to wait or take another option.
As a rider, I want an upfront fare before confirming so that I am not surprised by the bill.
As a rider, I want to be matched within a few seconds so that I am not left wondering.
As a rider, I want to watch my driver approach on a live map so that I can be at the curb on time.
As a rider, I want to share my live trip with family so that someone knows where I am.
As a rider, I want to be charged exactly once even if my app crashes or retries so that I trust the service.
As a rider, I want to cancel free of charge within a grace window so that a mistake does not cost me.
As a driver, I want to receive one clear offer at a time with pickup distance and fare so that I can decide in 15 seconds.
As a driver, I want navigation to the pickup and then the drop so that I do not need another app.
As a driver, I want my trip to continue even when my network drops in a tunnel so that I am paid for the full distance.
As a driver, I want to see surge heatmaps so that I can move to where demand is.
As a driver, I want to rate riders and see my rating breakdown so that bad behaviour has consequences.
As a city ops manager, I want to cap surge and create event pickup zones so that big events do not become a PR problem.
As a support agent, I want the full state history of a trip so that I can resolve a dispute with facts.
functional: Driver goes online/offline; while online, the app streams location every 4 s (every 1-2 s while on trip for smoother tracking).
Rider app shows nearby available cars by product (Go, Sedan, XL, Auto) refreshed every 3-5 s.
Fare quote: given pickup and drop, return upfront fare, surge multiplier and pickup ETA; quote valid for 2-5 minutes with a signed quote id.
Ride request with idempotency key; creates a trip in REQUESTED and starts matching.
Dispatch: find candidates, rank by ETA and other features, offer to one driver at a time (or batch-assign), with 15 s accept timeout and re-dispatch on decline/timeout.
Driver accept/decline; on accept, trip moves to MATCHED and both apps get each other's details.
Live tracking: rider sees driver position and updated ETA during ARRIVING and ON_TRIP.
Trip lifecycle: arrived, start (with optional PIN), end, cancel by rider/driver with reason and fee rules.
Fare computation at end: upfront fare honoured unless route materially changed; tolls and waiting time added.
Payments: pre-authorisation at request, capture on completion, tips, refunds, driver payouts, cash trips recorded as driver-owed commission.
Ratings: both sides rate 1-5 after trip, with tags; rolling average over last 500 trips.
Notifications: push for offers (driver), driver arriving (rider), receipts, safety alerts.
Surge pricing per H3 cell per minute with city caps and manual overrides.
Safety: SOS button, trip sharing link, route-deviation detection, PIN verification.
Ops tooling: airport FIFO queues, geofences, incentive campaigns, city config.

assumptions: 25M trips/day globally (Uber reports about 30M+ trips/day including deliveries).
5M drivers online at global peak, 1.5M in the busiest region.
Ping interval 4 s while available, 2 s while on trip; ping payload about 100 bytes (driver id, lat, lng, heading, speed, accuracy, timestamp, state).
Peak-to-average ratio of 3x daily, 10x on New Year's Eve in hot cities.
Rider app sessions: 3M concurrent at peak, each polling nearby cars every 5 s.
Average trip 20 minutes and 8 km; 20 candidate drivers ranked per request.
Persistent connections: drivers + riders with app open, about 8M concurrent.
math: Location writes: 5M drivers / 4 s = 1.25M pings/s at peak (Uber designed its geo index for about 1M writes/s).
Ingest bandwidth: 1.25M x 100 B = 125 MB/s = 1 Gbps inbound; about 10.8 TB/day raw if every ping were kept for a full day at peak rate, ~4-5 TB/day realistic average.
Geo index memory: 5M drivers x ~200 B (position, state, product, cell, ts) = 1 GB. The whole live world fits in RAM many times over; sharding is for write throughput and blast radius, not for size.
Ride requests: 25M/day / 86,400 = ~290/s average, ~900/s daily peak, ~3,000/s NYE global, maybe 300/s in one hot city.
ETA calls: 3,000 req/s x 20 candidates = 60k route queries/s at NYE peak for dispatch, plus quotes (~5 per trip) = 15k/s; CH queries at ~1 ms each = ~75 cores, provision 10x.
Nearby-cars reads: 3M sessions / 5 s = 600k geo reads/s, more than the dispatch reads; serve from replicas.
Gateways: 8M connections / 50k per node = 160 nodes; run ~400 across regions for N+1 zone headroom.
Trip storage: 25M x 5 KB = 125 GB/day, ~45 TB/year before replication (x3 = 135 TB).
Trip trails: 25M trips x 20 min x 30 pings/min x 40 B = 600 GB/day compressed to ~150 GB in the data lake.
Kafka: pings + trip events + app events = ~2M msgs/s peak; at 3x replication and 200 B average that is ~1.2 GB/s cluster write, ~100 TB/day before compaction.
Payments: 25M auths + 25M captures = 50M PSP calls/day = ~600/s average; ledger entries ~4 per trip = 100M rows/day.
capacity.summary: The system is dominated by a 1.25M/s stream of tiny, overwrite-only location writes and ~600k/s nearby-car reads, both of which fit easily in memory (about 1 GB of live state) but need horizontal sharding for throughput. Transactional load is modest by comparison (thousands of trips/s, hundreds of PSP calls/s) but must be correct, so it lives in strongly consistent stores sized in the low hundreds of TB per year.

out_of_scope: UberEats restaurant and courier batching logic.
UberPool / shared rides route insertion (mentioned as an extension of batched matching).
Driver onboarding, background checks and document verification workflows.
Building base maps (we license OSM/commercial tiles and maintain our own overlays).
Corporate travel billing, vouchers and promotions engine details.

hld.overview: The system splits into a real-time plane and a transactional plane joined by Kafka. The real-time plane (gateways, location service, geo index, supply/demand, DISCO matcher, ETA) is in-memory, sharded by city and H3 cell with Ringpop-style consistent hashing and SWIM gossip membership, and is optimised for latency and availability: if a node dies, drivers' next pings rebuild its state within seconds. The transactional plane (trip service, payments, ledger, ratings) runs on a Raft-replicated, strongly consistent document store (Docstore-style, MySQL underneath) and treats every external effect as idempotent. Each city is homed in one region (its cell) with a warm standby region; global services (identity, payments ledger, maps data) replicate across regions. Kafka carries every location ping and every state change to surge pricing (Flink), fraud, ETA model training (Michelangelo-style) and the data lake.

components.name: Rider app
components.responsibility: Quote, request, live map, payment method, ratings; holds an idempotency key per request and resumes trip state from the server on reconnect.

components.name: Driver app
components.responsibility: Online/offline, GPS streaming with on-device filtering (Kalman smoothing, accuracy gating), offer UI with 15 s timer, navigation, offline buffering of pings and trip events, stores encrypted trip digest.

components.name: Edge gateway
components.responsibility: TLS termination, auth tokens, per-user and per-device rate limits, persistent connection management (WebSocket/MQTT), connection registry (user -> gateway node) so any service can push to a client.

components.name: Location service
components.responsibility: Validate pings (timestamps, speed sanity, spoof heuristics), map-match to roads, update the geo index with latest position, append raw ping to Kafka; forwards on-trip pings to the rider's connection.

components.name: Geo index
components.responsibility: In-memory map from H3 cell -> set of driver entries (id, position, state, product, ts) plus driver -> cell reverse map; sharded by city and cell on a Ringpop ring; answers kRing nearest queries in under 5 ms.

components.name: Supply service
components.responsibility: Owns driver state machine (OFFLINE, AVAILABLE, OFFERED, EN_ROUTE, ON_TRIP), vehicle capabilities, seats; holds the driver lease and fencing token that prevent double assignment.

components.name: Demand service
components.responsibility: Accepts ride requests, validates quote id and payment eligibility, creates the trip, hands the request to the matcher, drives re-dispatch on decline or timeout.

components.name: DISCO matcher
components.responsibility: Per city shard: gather candidates, rank by ETA and features (acceptance probability, heading, trip continuation), then greedy offer or batch bipartite assignment every 1-2 s; can revise future plans.

components.name: ETA / routing service
components.responsibility: Road graph with contraction hierarchies and live traffic edge weights; many-to-one ETA matrices for dispatch; ML residual correction (DeepETA-like) on top of the routing ETA.

components.name: Pricing service + surge job
components.responsibility: Flink job aggregates supply and demand per H3 cell per minute and writes multipliers to a KV store; quote API computes upfront fare = base + time + distance x multiplier, signs the quote.

components.name: Trip service
components.responsibility: Authoritative trip state machine with versioned, conditional transitions in Docstore; writes outbox events; exposes trip history for support.

components.name: Payments service + ledger
components.responsibility: Saga orchestrator (Cadence-style workflow) for authorize, capture, void, refund, payout; idempotency store; double-entry ledger; reconciliation with PSP settlement files.

components.name: Notification service
components.responsibility: Delivers via live connection first, then APNs/FCM push, then SMS fallback for critical messages (driver arriving, SOS).

components.name: Ratings and reputation
components.responsibility: Collect post-trip ratings, compute rolling averages asynchronously, feed matching (avoid low-rated pairs) and deactivation review.

components.name: Fraud and safety
components.responsibility: Streaming rules and ML on pings and trip events: GPS spoof detection, collusion graphs, payment fraud scoring at request time, route deviation alerts.

components.name: Kafka + stream platform
components.responsibility: Regional clusters replicated by uReplicator into aggregate clusters; topics for pings, trip events, payments events; feeds Flink, fraud, data lake.

components.name: Control plane / city config
components.responsibility: City -> region homing, geofences, airport queues, surge caps, feature flags; failover orchestration.

flows.name: Driver location ingestion
steps: Driver app samples GPS at 1 Hz, smooths on device, sends one ping every 4 s (2 s on trip) over the persistent connection; batches up to 3 pings if the network was down.
Gateway authenticates the session (already done at connect time), applies a per-driver rate limit (e.g. max 2 pings/s) and forwards to the Location service shard for the driver's city.
Location service drops pings older than the last accepted timestamp (out-of-order), rejects impossible jumps (>200 km/h implied speed), map-matches to the road segment.

It computes the H3 res-9 cell; if the cell changed, it removes the driver from the old cell set and adds to the new one (both may be on different shards: done as two idempotent ops keyed by driver id + ts).
If the driver is on a trip, the position is forwarded to the rider's gateway node via the connection registry for the live map.
Ping is appended asynchronously to Kafka topic driver-locations (partitioned by driver_id) for trails, ETA traffic estimation, surge and fraud.

flows.name: Quote and request to match
steps: Rider opens app; nearby-cars query hits a geo index replica for kRing(k=2) around the rider's res-8 cell; returns up to 10 car icons, refreshed every 5 s.
Rider enters drop; Quote API reads the surge multiplier for the pickup cell (KV, < 5 ms), gets route distance/time from ETA service, computes upfront fare, returns a signed quote_id valid for 5 min.
Rider taps Request with idempotency key K; Demand service creates trip T in REQUESTED (insert-if-absent on K) and kicks off payment authorisation for the estimate.
Matcher queries the geo index for AVAILABLE drivers of the right product within kRing k=2, expanding to k=4 and k=6 if fewer than 5 candidates.
ETA service returns a many-to-one road ETA for up to 20 candidates in one call (~10 ms).
Matcher ranks (ETA plus acceptance probability, heading, destination filters) and attempts CAS AVAILABLE -> OFFERED with lease 15 s on the top driver; on CAS failure it moves to the next candidate.
Offer is pushed to the driver; on accept the driver goes OFFERED -> EN_ROUTE and trip goes REQUESTED -> MATCHED with a version check; both apps get push updates.
On decline or lease expiry, the driver returns to AVAILABLE and the matcher re-dispatches excluding that driver; after 3 rounds or 60 s the rider sees no cars available.

flows.name: Trip progress and completion
steps: Driver taps Arrived; trip MATCHED -> ARRIVING -> ARRIVED; rider notified via live connection and push.
Driver enters rider PIN, taps Start; trip -> ON_TRIP; ping rate goes to every 2 s and pings are tagged with trip_id for the trail.
During the trip, route deviation and long-stop detectors run on the stream for safety alerts; ETA to drop is recomputed every 30 s.
Driver taps End; trip -> COMPLETED with final distance/time computed from the map-matched trail (server-side, not the phone's odometer).
Trip service writes the transition and an outbox event TripCompleted in the same transaction; the outbox relay publishes to Kafka.

Payments saga consumes TripCompleted, computes final fare (upfront fare unless route changed >X%), captures with idempotency key capture:T, writes ledger entries, sends receipt; both sides get rating prompts.

flows.name: Surge computation
steps: Flink reads ride-requests, app-opens (eyeballs) and driver-locations from the aggregate Kafka cluster.
Keys each event by H3 res-8 cell; 1-minute tumbling windows (or 2-minute sliding with 30 s hop) count demand and available supply, with a 10 s watermark for late events.
Applies smoothing over neighbouring cells (kRing 1) and over time (EWMA) to avoid flicker; ML model predicts short-term demand; applies city caps.
Writes multiplier per cell with a TTL of 2-3 minutes to a replicated KV store; the quote API reads it; drivers see a heatmap.
Only the primary region's job writes; other regions compute the same thing from the aggregate cluster as hot standbys (active-active compute, single writer).

flows.name: Region failover mid-trip
steps: Health checks and the control plane declare region A unhealthy for city C; DNS/edge routing for C's clients moves to region B (TTL 30 s, plus client-side failover list).
Clients reconnect to region B gateways; drivers' next pings rebuild B's geo index in 4-8 s.
For an in-flight trip unknown to B (replication lag), the driver app uploads its encrypted trip digest; Trip service validates the signature and recreates or reconciles the trip.
Payments captures queued in A are replayed from the replicated outbox/Kafka in B; idempotency keys make the replay safe.

hld.data_flow: Hot path writes (pings) go client -> gateway -> location service -> in-memory geo index, with a copy to Kafka; nothing on the hot path waits for a disk. Hot path reads (nearby cars, dispatch candidates) read the geo index; dispatch then writes a lease to the driver state store (strongly consistent per driver) and a transition to the trip store (Raft). Every durable change emits an outbox event to Kafka; Kafka fans out to pricing (Flink -> surge KV), payments (saga -> PSP -> ledger), notifications, fraud, ratings aggregation and the data lake (HDFS/Hive) that trains ETA, acceptance and demand models offline. Surge multipliers and model outputs flow back into the hot path as cached reads.

algorithms.name: Nearby search with expanding H3 kRing
algorithms.explain: Convert the rider point to an H3 res-9 cell (~174 m edge). Ask for drivers in kRing(cell, k) which is all cells within k hex steps; k=2 covers roughly a 0.9 km radius. If fewer than minCount AVAILABLE drivers of the product are found, grow k. Distances are then refined with haversine and finally road ETA. Hex neighbours are all equidistant, so the ring approximates a circle better than geohash squares.

algorithms.name: Driver reservation with lease and fencing token
algorithms.explain: Prevents double assignment. The driver state row is changed only by compare-and-set on version. Each successful reservation gets a monotonically increasing fencing token; any later write (accept, start trip) must present the current token, so a slow matcher holding an expired lease cannot overwrite a newer assignment.
algorithms.pseudocode:
function tryReserve(driverId, tripId, ttl=15s):
  row = store.get(driverId)              # linearizable read
  if row.state != AVAILABLE and not (row.state == OFFERED and row.lease < now):
    return None
  token = row.fencing_token + 1
  ok = store.cas(driverId, expectVersion=row.version,
                 new={state: OFFERED, trip_id: tripId,
                      lease: now + ttl, fencing_token: token,
                      version: row.version + 1})
  return token if ok else None           # lost race -> try next driver

function accept(driverId, tripId, token):
  row = store.get(driverId)
  if row.fencing_token != token or row.lease < now: return 409
  store.cas(driverId, row.version, {state: EN_ROUTE, version: +1})
  trips.transition(tripId, MATCHED, expectedVersion)

algorithms.name: Batched bipartite matching (Hungarian / min-cost assignment)
algorithms.explain: Every 1-2 s per dispatch zone, collect open requests R and available drivers D. Build a cost matrix c[r][d] = pickup ETA plus penalties (low acceptance probability, long dead-head after drop, rating mismatch), with infinity where ETA exceeds a cap. Solve min-cost assignment. Hungarian is O(n^3), fine for a few hundred per zone; larger zones use auction algorithms or min-cost flow on a sparse graph. Batching beats greedy because greedy gives the nearest driver to whoever asked first, stealing the only nearby driver of a later rider.

algorithms.name: ETA with contraction hierarchies and live traffic
algorithms.explain: Preprocess the road graph by contracting nodes in order of importance and adding shortcut edges that preserve shortest paths. A query runs a bidirectional Dijkstra that only relaxes edges going up the hierarchy, settling a few hundred nodes instead of millions, so continental queries take about 1 ms. Live traffic changes edge weights; full CH re-preprocessing is too slow, so a customizable variant (CCH / CRP) keeps the topology fixed and recomputes only the metric in seconds. An ML model then corrects the route ETA residual.

algorithms.name: Surge multiplier from streaming aggregation
algorithms.explain: Per H3 res-8 cell and 1-minute window, compute demand (requests plus weighted app opens) and supply (available drivers plus drivers finishing trips nearby soon). Ratio maps to a multiplier through a city-tuned curve, smoothed over neighbours and time to avoid flicker, and capped.
algorithms.pseudocode:
stream.keyBy(h3_res8).window(Tumbling(60s)).allowedLateness(10s):
  demand = count(requests) + 0.3 * count(app_opens_with_dest)
  supply = count(distinct available drivers) + 0.5 * count(trips_ending_in_5min)
  raw = curve_city(demand / max(supply, 1))   # e.g. 1.0 below ratio 1.2
  nb = mean(raw over kRing(cell,1))
  m = 0.6*raw + 0.4*nb
  m = ewma(prev[cell], m, alpha=0.5)
  m = min(m, capFor(city)); m = round_to(m, 0.1)
  kv.put(cell, m, ttl=180s)   # only primary region writes

algorithms.name: Trip state machine with optimistic concurrency
algorithms.explain: Allowed transitions are a fixed table. Each update carries expected_version; the store applies it only if the version matches, so concurrent rider cancel and driver start cannot both win. The losing side receives 409 with current state and resolves (e.g. cancel after start becomes a normal trip end).

edge_cases.case: Two matchers try to offer the same driver to two riders at the same instant
edge_cases.handling: Only the CAS on the driver state row wins; the loser sees version mismatch and moves to its next candidate. Ringpop also routes a driver's reservations to one owner, so the race is rare, but correctness relies on the CAS plus fencing token, not on routing.

edge_cases.case: Driver accepts just as the 15 s lease expires and the trip was re-offered
edge_cases.handling: Accept carries the fencing token; the re-offer bumped the token, so the stale accept gets 409 'expired'. The driver app shows 'offer no longer available'.

edge_cases.case: Rider taps Request twice, or the app retries after a timeout
edge_cases.handling: Same Idempotency-Key -> insert-if-absent returns the original trip. A different key while a trip is active hits the one-active-trip-per-rider constraint and returns the existing trip.

edge_cases.case: Rider cancels at the same moment the driver taps Start
edge_cases.handling: Both send expected_version; one commits first. If Start won, cancel returns 409 with ON_TRIP and the app offers 'end trip' instead; if Cancel won, Start gets 409 and the driver app returns to available. No double state.

edge_cases.case: Driver's network drops in a tunnel for 3 minutes mid-trip
edge_cases.handling: App keeps recording GPS locally and queues trip events; server keeps the trip ON_TRIP (no auto-cancel on silence during a trip); on reconnect the buffered pings are uploaded in seq order and the trail gap is filled by map-matching the route between last and next points for fare.

edge_cases.case: Driver goes silent while AVAILABLE (app killed, phone died)
edge_cases.handling: Geo index entry expires after 30 s without a ping so dispatch stops seeing the driver; the supply state flips to OFFLINE after 2 minutes; if an offer was pending, its lease expires and the request re-dispatches.

edge_cases.case: GPS drift: urban canyon puts the driver on a parallel street or across a river
edge_cases.handling: On-device Kalman filter plus server-side map matching (HMM over road segments) using heading and speed; accuracy_m > 50 m pings are down-weighted; fare uses map-matched distance, not raw point-to-point.

edge_cases.case: GPS spoofing apps fake a driver's location near the airport to jump the queue
edge_cases.handling: Teleport checks (implied speed), mock-location flags, device attestation, cell-tower/Wi-Fi consistency, and comparing with accelerometer signals; offending accounts are removed from queues and reviewed.

edge_cases.case: Out-of-order pings (older ping arrives after a newer one)
edge_cases.handling: Each ping has device seq and timestamp; the location service ignores any ping with seq <= last accepted, so the index never moves a driver backwards.

edge_cases.case: Device clock skew of minutes on cheap phones
edge_cases.handling: Server stamps receive time; device ts used only for ordering within a session and corrected by an offset estimated at connect time (NTP-like handshake).

edge_cases.case: Hot cell: 30,000 people leave a cricket stadium at once
edge_cases.handling: Event geofence with dedicated pickup zones; requests queue in a FIFO per zone; batched matching over the zone; surge rises to pull supply; the geo shard for that area is split to a finer resolution or replicated for reads.

edge_cases.case: Driver crosses a shard boundary between two pings
edge_cases.handling: Move is two idempotent ops: remove from old cell owner, add to new owner, both keyed by (driver_id, seq). A transient duplicate is harmless because candidates are de-duplicated by driver_id and the lease is authoritative.

edge_cases.case: Rider's pickup is near a city or region boundary
edge_cases.handling: Matching uses the rider's home city shard but candidate search spans the kRing across the boundary; cross-city drivers are allowed if regulation permits; the trip is homed where it was requested.

edge_cases.case: No drivers within reach (k=6 exhausted)
edge_cases.handling: Return 'no cars available' quickly rather than holding the rider; keep the request in a short waitlist (60 s) in case a nearby driver frees up; feed the unmet demand to surge and supply-positioning.

edge_cases.case: PSP times out on capture: did the charge happen?
edge_cases.handling: Mark PENDING, never retry with a new key. Retry with the same idempotency key or query PSP status by key; reconciliation against the settlement file closes anything still unknown within 24 h.

edge_cases.case: Card authorisation fails after the driver is already en route
edge_cases.handling: Auth happens at request time before matching; if a later incremental auth fails, switch to backup method or cash, and the trip still completes; debt is recorded against the rider account.

edge_cases.case: Final fare exceeds the authorised amount (long detour, tolls)
edge_cases.handling: Incremental authorisation or capture within PSP's over-capture tolerance; otherwise capture the authorised part and charge the remainder as a separate idempotent charge.

edge_cases.case: Duplicate TripCompleted events delivered by Kafka
edge_cases.handling: Payments consumer checks processed event_id and idempotency key capture:{trip_id}; the second delivery is a no-op that returns the stored result.

edge_cases.case: Region fails between trip start and trip end
edge_cases.handling: Trip row is replicated cross-region; if it lagged, the driver's encrypted trip digest recreates it; end event processed in the new region; capture keyed by trip_id so a replay from the old region's outbox later is harmless.

edge_cases.case: Surge job stops writing (Flink failure)
edge_cases.handling: KV entries have a 3 minute TTL; quote API falls back to last known multiplier decayed toward 1.0x, capped; standby region's job is promoted as writer.

edge_cases.case: Upfront quote expires while the rider deliberates
edge_cases.handling: Request with expired quote returns 409 plus a fresh quote; the client shows the new price explicitly if it rose by more than a threshold.

edge_cases.case: Driver and rider collude to create fake trips for incentives
edge_cases.handling: Graph features (same devices, same pairs repeatedly, short loops, no movement variance) in the fraud model; payouts for flagged trips held for review.

edge_cases.case: Rider requests from a place the car cannot reach (inside a mall, wrong side of a highway)
edge_cases.handling: Snap pickup to the nearest suggested pickup point learned from historical pickups; ETA computed to the snapped point; driver sees the exact spot.

edge_cases.case: Airport queue: a driver leaves the lot and returns
edge_cases.handling: Geofence exit removes the driver from the FIFO after a grace period; position in queue is not restored to stop gaming; queue lives in a strongly consistent store.

edge_cases.case: Thundering herd on reconnect after a gateway node restarts
edge_cases.handling: Clients reconnect with exponential backoff plus full jitter (base 1 s, cap 30 s); gateways admit with a token bucket and shed with Retry-After.

edge_cases.case: Rating submitted twice or very late
edge_cases.handling: Upsert keyed by (trip_id, rater_role) with a 7 day window; aggregation is a recompute over the last 500 so late arrivals are naturally included.

edge_cases.case: A matcher node is partitioned but still believes it owns its cells
edge_cases.handling: It may compute matches, but it cannot reserve drivers: the lease store is CP and the stale node's CAS fails or its token is stale. Correctness is preserved; only latency is lost until SWIM marks it faulty.

tech_stack.name: H3 (hexagonal hierarchical spatial index)
tech_stack.overview: Uber's open-source grid that tiles the earth with hexagons at 16 resolutions; each cell has a 64-bit id, every child is ~1/7 the area of its parent.
tech_stack.why: Uniform neighbour distance makes kRing searches and surge smoothing natural; cell ids are cheap shard and aggregation keys.
tech_stack.alternatives: Geohash (simple string prefixes but square cells with edge discontinuities), S2 (Uber's earlier choice, exact hierarchical containment on a Hilbert curve), PostGIS R-tree (great for ad hoc queries, too slow for 1M writes/s).

tech_stack.name: Ringpop-style consistent hashing + SWIM
tech_stack.overview: An embedded library that puts service instances on a hash ring and uses SWIM gossip for membership so requests are forwarded to the owner of a key.
tech_stack.why: Lets stateful in-memory services (geo index, dispatch) shard by key without a central coordinator and rebalance automatically when nodes join or die.
tech_stack.alternatives: Central shard map in ZooKeeper/etcd (simpler reasoning, coordinator dependency), Kubernetes StatefulSets with static assignment (no automatic rebalance), Envoy ring-hash load balancing (no in-process forwarding).

tech_stack.name: Apache Kafka (+ uReplicator)
tech_stack.overview: Distributed, partitioned, replicated commit log; Uber runs trillions of messages per day with regional and aggregate clusters.
tech_stack.why: Decouples the hot path from every consumer (surge, fraud, payments, lake), gives replay, ordering per key (driver_id, trip_id) and cross-region replication.
tech_stack.alternatives: Pulsar (tiered storage and geo-replication built in), Kinesis/PubSub (managed, less control), RabbitMQ (not built for this throughput or replay).

tech_stack.name: Apache Flink
tech_stack.overview: Stateful stream processor with event-time windows, watermarks and checkpointed exactly-once state.
tech_stack.why: Surge needs per-cell windowed aggregation with seconds-level freshness; Uber runs surge pricing as Flink jobs reading Kafka.
tech_stack.alternatives: Spark Structured Streaming (micro-batch, higher latency), Kafka Streams (simpler, library-only, weaker for very large state), Samza/Storm (older).

tech_stack.name: Docstore (Schemaless evolution) on MySQL
tech_stack.overview: Uber's distributed document database: partitions of 3-5 nodes replicated with Raft, MySQL as storage engine, strict serializability per partition.
tech_stack.why: Trips, payments and driver state need CP semantics, conditional writes and ACID transactions for the outbox pattern at very high scale.
tech_stack.alternatives: Spanner/CockroachDB (global serializable transactions, higher write latency across regions), Cassandra (AP, LWT is slow), sharded Postgres (operational burden).

tech_stack.name: Redis / in-memory KV
tech_stack.overview: In-memory data structures with replication; also used as a surge multiplier cache and connection registry.
tech_stack.why: Sub-millisecond reads for surge lookups and session routing on the quote and push paths.
tech_stack.alternatives: Memcached (simpler, no structures), Aerospike (SSD-backed, larger data), local in-process caches with pub/sub invalidation.

tech_stack.name: Routing engine with contraction hierarchies (OSRM-like) + DeepETA
tech_stack.overview: Graph search over a preprocessed road network with traffic-aware weights, then an ML model that learns the residual between routing ETA and real arrivals.
tech_stack.why: Dispatch needs tens of thousands of ETA queries per second at millisecond latency, and accuracy directly drives cancellations.
tech_stack.alternatives: Plain Dijkstra/A* (too slow at scale), commercial routing APIs (cost and latency per call), pure ML ETA without routing (poor generalisation).

tech_stack.name: WebSockets / MQTT over TLS + APNs/FCM
tech_stack.overview: Persistent bidirectional connections for pings, offers and live tracking, with platform push as fallback when the app is backgrounded.
tech_stack.why: Offers need sub-second delivery; polling at 1 s for 8M clients would be 8M req/s of mostly empty responses.
tech_stack.alternatives: Long polling (works through every proxy, more overhead), server-sent events (server to client only), HTTP/2 or gRPC streams (good, needs proxy support).

tech_stack.name: Cadence / Temporal workflows
tech_stack.overview: Uber-built durable workflow engine: workflow state is persisted after every step and replayed deterministically after crashes.
tech_stack.why: The payment saga (authorize, capture, void, refund, payout) spans minutes to days and must survive restarts with retries and compensations.
tech_stack.alternatives: Hand-rolled state machine + cron pollers (error prone), AWS Step Functions (managed, vendor lock-in), choreography over Kafka only (harder to see the whole saga).

tech_stack.name: Michelangelo (ML platform)
tech_stack.overview: Uber's end-to-end ML platform: feature store, training, deployment and online prediction serving.
tech_stack.why: ETA residuals, acceptance probability, demand forecast, fraud scores all need consistent online/offline features and low-latency serving.

tech_stack.name: HDFS/Hive + Pinot
tech_stack.overview: Data lake for trails and events; Pinot for real-time OLAP dashboards.
tech_stack.why: City ops need minute-fresh supply/demand dashboards; models and disputes need long history.
tech_stack.alternatives: Druid/ClickHouse for OLAP, Iceberg/Delta on object storage for the lake.

tech_stack.name: TChannel / gRPC with backup requests
tech_stack.overview: Multiplexed RPC with tracing, deadlines and request hedging.
tech_stack.why: Tail latency control: send a backup request to a second replica after p95 delay and cancel the loser.
tech_stack.alternatives: Plain HTTP/1.1 JSON (simpler, slower), Thrift over HTTP.

tech_stack.name: PSP (Stripe / Adyen / Razorpay class)
tech_stack.overview: External processor for cards, wallets, UPI; supports idempotency keys, auth, capture, refunds and settlement files.
tech_stack.why: Card network compliance (PCI) and local payment rails are not our core business.
tech_stack.alternatives: Multiple PSPs with smart routing (resilience, more reconciliation work), direct acquiring (cheaper at huge scale, heavy compliance).

tech_stack.name: Envoy / edge load balancers + GeoDNS
tech_stack.overview: L4/L7 proxies and DNS steering clients to their city's home region.
tech_stack.why: City-to-region homing and fast failover by changing routing, not clients.
tech_stack.alternatives: Anycast with BGP only, client-side region lists (used together).

concepts.name: Geospatial indexing (geohash, quadtree, S2, H3)
concepts.explain: A geospatial index answers 'which points are near here' without scanning every point. All practical schemes discretise the earth into cells and give each cell an id, so a proximity query becomes 'look up these few cells'. Geohash interleaves the bits of latitude and longitude and base-32 encodes them; longer strings mean smaller rectangles (5 chars about 4.9 km, 6 chars about 1.2 x 0.6 km, 7 chars about 153 m). Shared prefixes usually mean nearness, which makes it easy to store in any sorted key-value store, but two points a metre apart across a boundary can share no prefix, so every search must also check the 8 neighbouring cells. A quadtree recursively splits a square into four children until each leaf holds at most N points; it adapts to density (tiny leaves downtown, huge ones in the desert) but must split and merge as objects move. Google's S2 projects the sphere onto the six faces of a cube and orders cells along a Hilbert curve; ids are 64-bit integers across 31 levels and a cell's children share its id prefix, so containment and range covering are exact and cheap. Uber's H3 projects onto an icosahedron and tiles it with hexagons at 16 resolutions, each child about one seventh of its parent's area, with 12 unavoidable pentagons placed mostly in oceans. Hexagons have one neighbour distance instead of two (squares) or three (triangles), so a k-ring of cells approximates a circle and flows between neighbours are uniform. H3 parent/child containment is approximate, unlike S2. R-trees (PostGIS) index arbitrary shapes and are ideal for polygon queries but are expensive to update at millions of writes per second.
concepts.in_this_design: Each driver ping is converted to an H3 res-9 cell (about 174 m edge). The geo index is a hash map of cell -> driver set, so a move is O(1). Candidate search takes gridDisk/kRing around the rider's cell and widens k until enough drivers are found. Surge uses res-8 cells (about 0.74 km^2) for aggregation and smoothing across neighbours. Uber's earlier dispatch used S2 level 12 cells as shard keys; H3 replaced squares where uniform neighbours matter.
key_points: A geo index turns 'near me' into 'these few cell ids', which any hash map or KV store can serve.
Geohash: simple prefix strings, edge discontinuities, always check 8 neighbours.
Quadtree: adapts to density but rebalancing moving points is costly.
S2: Hilbert-curve ordered 64-bit cells with exact hierarchy; great for coverings and sharding.
H3: hexagons, 16 resolutions, equidistant neighbours, kRing search, ideal for movement and smoothing.

qa.q: Why are hexagons better than squares for ride-hailing?
qa.a: Every neighbour of a hexagon is the same distance from its centre, so expanding search rings grow like circles and aggregations like surge smoothing treat all neighbours equally. With squares, diagonal neighbours are 1.41x farther, which distorts both. Hexagons also reduce quantisation error as vehicles move through a city.

qa.q: When would you choose S2 over H3?
qa.a: When you need exact hierarchical containment or efficient covering of arbitrary regions with cell ranges, for example indexing geofences or sharding by contiguous id ranges along the Hilbert curve. H3 children do not perfectly tile their parent, so it is weaker for exact region coverings.

qa.q: Why not a quadtree for drivers?
qa.a: Quadtrees shine for static, unevenly distributed points. Drivers move every 4 seconds, so you would constantly split and merge nodes and lock subtrees under write load. A fixed grid of cells gives O(1) updates; density is handled by choosing the resolution and by splitting hot shards, not the tree.

qa.q: How do you handle a search near a cell edge?
qa.a: Never search only the rider's own cell. Search the ring of neighbours (8 for geohash, kRing for H3) and then refine with true distance and finally road ETA. Cell membership is only a coarse filter.

concepts.name: Location update ingestion and write-heavy scaling
concepts.explain: Write-heavy systems are bounded by how much work each write costs. The usual levers are: make each write cheaper (in memory instead of disk, overwrite instead of append, no secondary index maintenance on the hot path), spread writes across more machines (sharding), reduce the number of writes (client-side batching, adaptive rates, dropping redundant updates) and move durable work off the hot path (write the latest value synchronously, stream the history asynchronously through a log). A location ping is a special kind of write: it is idempotent and superseded, since only the newest value matters for matching, and the previous value has no business meaning once overwritten. That means you can lose a ping without harm, you can rebuild the current state from the next round of pings, and you do not need consensus or fsync for it. History still matters for fares, safety and traffic models, so it goes to an append-only log that batches and compresses well. On the client, GPS is sampled more often than it is sent, filtered with a Kalman filter, and sent less often when stationary. Backpressure matters too: if a shard falls behind, the right response is to drop stale pings (keep only the newest per driver) rather than queue them, because a queued old ping is worse than no ping.
concepts.in_this_design: 5M online drivers pinging every 4 s gives 1.25M writes per second, about 125 MB/s. The location service keeps latest position only, in memory, sharded by city and cell; the raw ping goes to Kafka partitioned by driver_id for trails, ETA traffic models and fraud. Pings carry a sequence number so late arrivals are dropped. Rates adapt: 4 s available, 2 s on trip, slower when stationary or on low battery.
key_points: Latest-value state is overwrite-only and rebuildable, so keep it in memory and skip consensus.
History goes to a log (Kafka) asynchronously; nothing on the hot path waits for disk.
Under overload, drop stale pings, never queue them.
Client-side filtering and adaptive rates are the cheapest scaling lever.
Sequence numbers make ingestion idempotent and order-safe.

qa.q: Your location service is falling behind. What do you do first?
qa.a: Shed the right load: collapse queued pings per driver to the newest, lower the ping interval remotely via config pushed on the socket (4 s to 6 s), and stop forwarding non-essential copies. Then scale out shards for the hot city. Queueing old pings only adds lag.

qa.q: Why not write each ping to Cassandra?
qa.a: You could, Cassandra handles high write rates, but you pay replication, commit log and compaction for data whose current value you only need for seconds. Matching would still need an in-memory index for fast spatial reads. Kafka plus a data lake keeps history cheaper.

qa.q: How do you rebuild state after a node dies?
qa.a: Do nothing special: every available driver pings within 4 s, so the new owner's index is complete after one interval. Optionally warm it from a follower replica or by replaying the last 10 s of the Kafka topic for those cells.

qa.q: How do you reduce battery drain on the driver app?
qa.a: Sample GPS frequently but transmit less, batch when stationary, use fused location providers, keep one persistent connection instead of many HTTP requests, and compress or delta-encode positions.

concepts.name: Consistent hashing (Ringpop-style application-layer sharding)
concepts.explain: Naive sharding with hash(key) mod N remaps almost every key when N changes, which for an in-memory service means rebuilding nearly all state on every deploy or failure. Consistent hashing places both nodes and keys on a ring of hash values (for example 0 to 2^32); a key belongs to the first node clockwise from its hash. When a node leaves, only its keys move, to its successor; when a node joins, it takes keys only from one neighbour. To avoid uneven arcs, each physical node is placed at many points (virtual nodes, typically 100-200), which smooths load and lets heterogeneous machines take proportional shares. Variants include rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing, which needs no ring, and jump consistent hash, which is compact but needs numbered buckets. Ringpop, which Uber open-sourced, embeds a consistent hash ring inside every instance of a service. Any instance can receive a request; it looks up the owner of the request's key on its local copy of the ring and either handles it or forwards it to the owner. The ring's membership comes from a gossip protocol, so there is no central coordinator. This makes stateful services horizontally scalable, but because membership views converge eventually, two nodes can briefly disagree about ownership; the design must tolerate that.
concepts.in_this_design: The geo index and dispatch are sharded by key on a Ringpop-style ring: the key is city plus the H3 res-6 parent of a cell, so a kRing query touches one or two owners. Pings for a cell are forwarded to its owner; a node failure moves only its arcs. Because ownership can briefly overlap, the driver lease store, not the ring, guarantees no double assignment.
key_points: Consistent hashing moves only about 1/N of keys when membership changes.
Virtual nodes even out load and handle heterogeneous machines.
Ringpop = ring + gossip membership + request forwarding embedded in each service.
Ring ownership is eventually consistent; never use it alone as a lock.
Choose the key for locality of queries (cell parent), not just even spread.

qa.q: What problem do virtual nodes solve?
qa.a: With one point per node the arcs are random and some nodes get several times the average load. With hundreds of points per node the variance shrinks, and when a node fails its load is spread across many successors instead of dumped on one.

qa.q: Why shard by cell parent rather than driver_id?
qa.a: Queries are spatial: 'drivers near this point'. With driver_id hashing every nearby query fans out to all shards. With cell-parent keys a query touches one or two shards. The cost is hot spots, handled by finer keys or replicas for busy areas.

qa.q: Two Ringpop nodes both think they own a cell. What breaks?
qa.a: Both may hold driver positions and both may compute matches, but both must reserve drivers through the CP lease store, so only one reservation per driver succeeds. Stale ownership costs duplicate work and some latency, not correctness.

qa.q: Rendezvous hashing vs ring?
qa.a: Rendezvous hashes the key with every node and picks the highest score; it needs no ring and gives perfect minimal movement, but lookup is O(N) unless you add structure. Rings give O(log N) lookups with virtual nodes and are what Ringpop and Dynamo-style systems use.

concepts.name: Gossip and membership (SWIM failure detection)
concepts.explain: A cluster without a central coordinator still needs every node to know who is alive. All-to-all heartbeats cost O(N^2) messages and false-positive rates grow with N. SWIM (Scalable Weakly-consistent Infection-style Membership, Das, Gupta and Motivala, 2002) separates failure detection from dissemination. Each protocol period, a node pings one random member. If no ack arrives in time, it asks k other members to ping the target indirectly (ping-req), which distinguishes a dead node from a lossy link between two particular nodes. If still nothing, the target is marked suspect rather than dead; the suspect state is gossiped, and the target can refute it by gossiping an alive message with a higher incarnation number. Only after a suspicion timeout is it declared faulty. Membership changes are piggybacked on the ping and ack messages themselves, spreading epidemically in O(log N) rounds, so per-node load is constant regardless of cluster size. The result is weakly consistent: different nodes may see different membership for a few seconds. HashiCorp's memberlist (Consul, Serf) and Uber's Ringpop both use SWIM with extensions such as Lifeguard tuning, which reduces false positives when the detecting node itself is slow.
concepts.in_this_design: Every geo index and dispatch instance runs SWIM to maintain the Ringpop ring. When a node dies, peers detect it within a few protocol periods (about 1 s each), suspect, then remove it; the ring recomputes and its cells move to successors. Uber reported Ringpop scaling to thousands of nodes with modified SWIM for faster convergence.
key_points: Ping one random member per period; ask k others to ping-req before suspecting.
Suspect state plus incarnation numbers cut false positives from slow nodes.
Updates piggyback on pings, so dissemination is O(log N) rounds with constant per-node load.
Membership is weakly consistent; design the data path to tolerate temporary disagreement.
Failure detection time is a tunable trade-off against false positives.

qa.q: Why does SWIM use indirect pings?
qa.a: A missed ack might be caused by a bad link between the prober and the target, not a dead target. Asking k other nodes to probe gives independent paths, so a node is only suspected when several paths fail, which lowers false positives without many extra messages.

qa.q: How long does it take to detect a failure?
qa.a: Roughly a few protocol periods plus the suspicion timeout. With a 1 s period, k=3 and a suspicion timeout of a few seconds, detection is typically 3-10 s; dissemination then takes O(log N) gossip rounds.

qa.q: What is the risk of tuning detection too aggressively?
qa.a: Garbage collection pauses or CPU spikes cause healthy nodes to be declared dead, which causes ring churn, state movement and more load, which causes more pauses: a flapping cascade. Lifeguard-style local health awareness and suspicion timeouts guard against it.

qa.q: Gossip vs a ZooKeeper-managed membership list?
qa.a: ZooKeeper gives one consistent view and simpler reasoning, but it is a central dependency whose session timeouts and write throughput bound the cluster. Gossip has no single point of failure and scales to thousands of nodes but only gives eventual agreement.

concepts.name: Sharding and partitioning by geography (city cells)
concepts.explain: Partitioning splits data and traffic so that each piece fits on one machine and failures stay local. The partition key decides everything: queries that include the key go to one partition, queries that do not must scatter-gather. Range partitioning keeps adjacent keys together (good for scans, risky for hot ranges); hash partitioning spreads load evenly but destroys locality; directory-based partitioning uses a lookup table that can be edited for rebalancing. Geography is a natural key for physical-world systems because almost every interaction is local: a rider in Chennai is never matched with a driver in Delhi. Partitioning by city gives isolation (a Mumbai incident cannot take down Bengaluru), aligns with regulation and operations (pricing, airport rules, tax are per city), and allows homing each city to the nearest datacenter. Geography is also extremely skewed: a megacity has thousands of times the load of a small town, and inside a city, a stadium or airport can be thousands of times a residential cell. So a geographic scheme needs a second level (cells within a city) and a way to split hot cells. A cell-based architecture takes this further: each cell is a full, independent copy of the stack serving a subset of cities, limiting blast radius.
concepts.in_this_design: The real-time plane is partitioned first by city (directory: city -> home region and cell), then by H3 res-6 parent within the city on a consistent hash ring. Trips are hash-partitioned by trip_id within the home region's store to avoid a hot shard per big city. Large cities get more shards; airports and stadiums get dedicated zones and FIFO queues.
key_points: Pick the partition key that matches the dominant query; for ride-hailing that is location.
Two levels: city (isolation, homing, regulation) then cell (throughput).
Geographic data is heavily skewed; plan for hot-cell splitting and replicas.
Use hash partitioning for entities accessed by id (trips), not by city.
A directory (city -> region/cell) makes rebalancing and failover a config change.

qa.q: Why not shard everything by city?
qa.a: A megacity would be a single huge shard, and a single city's trips would all land on one database. City is the right isolation and routing key, but within a city you need finer partitioning: spatial cells for the geo index and trip_id hashes for trip storage.

qa.q: A concert ends and one cell gets 50x load. What do you do?
qa.a: Split that cell's key to a finer resolution so it spans several owners, add read replicas for nearby-car queries, move matching for the venue into a dedicated zone with batched FIFO assignment, and lean on surge to pull in supply.

qa.q: How do you handle trips that cross city boundaries?
qa.a: The trip is homed where it was requested, so all state transitions stay with one owner. Location pings still update whichever cell the driver is in; the trip service does not care which geo shard the driver is on.

qa.q: What is a cell-based architecture and why use it here?
qa.a: A cell is a full, self-contained deployment of the stack (gateways, services, storage) that serves a subset of cities. Bugs, bad deploys and overload stay in one cell. You route by a thin global layer (city -> cell), deploy cell by cell, and fail a city over by changing that mapping.

concepts.name: Replication and quorum
concepts.explain: Replication keeps copies of data on several machines for durability and availability. Leader-based replication sends all writes through one leader that ships a log to followers; synchronous followers give durability at the cost of latency, asynchronous ones give speed at the risk of losing the last writes on failover. Consensus protocols such as Raft and Paxos commit a log entry once a majority (quorum) of replicas has it, so with 3 replicas the system survives 1 failure and with 5 it survives 2, and a new leader is guaranteed to have every committed entry. Leaderless (Dynamo-style) replication writes to N replicas and waits for W acks, reads from R; if R + W > N, every read quorum overlaps the latest write quorum, so N=3, W=2, R=2 is the classic setting. Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff keep writes available during partitions at the cost of possible conflicts, which need read repair, version vectors or last-writer-wins. Quorums give a durability and recency guarantee but not automatically linearizability; for compare-and-set you need consensus or a single leader. Placement matters: replicas in different availability zones survive a zone loss; across regions they survive a region loss but every synchronous commit pays the inter-region round trip, typically 30-150 ms.
concepts.in_this_design: Trips, driver leases and payments live in a Docstore-style store: each partition is a Raft group of 3-5 nodes spread across zones, MySQL as the engine, so a commit survives a zone loss and failover is automatic. Cross-region copies are asynchronous for trips (RPO under a second, backed by the driver digest) and synchronous for the payment ledger where RPO must be 0. The geo index uses one asynchronous follower per shard only to speed recovery.
key_points: Raft/Paxos: commit on majority; 2f+1 replicas tolerate f failures.
Dynamo quorum: R + W > N gives overlap; N=3, W=2, R=2 is the classic.
Quorum overlap alone is not linearizable CAS; use consensus or a leader for locks.
Synchronous cross-region replication costs a WAN round trip per commit; use it only for money.
Match replication strength to the cost of losing the data.

qa.q: Why use 5 replicas instead of 3 for the payment ledger?
qa.a: Five tolerates two simultaneous failures, for example one zone down for maintenance while another node fails. For money the extra storage and slightly slower commits are worth it; for trips, 3 is enough.

qa.q: With N=3, W=1, R=1, what goes wrong?
qa.a: Reads and writes may hit different replicas with no overlap, so a reader can see stale data indefinitely until anti-entropy catches up. Fine for counters on dashboards, unacceptable for driver state.

qa.q: Why not replicate the geo index synchronously across regions?
qa.a: It changes 1.25M times per second, is worthless after a few seconds, and rebuilds itself from the next pings. Synchronous replication would multiply cost and latency to protect data that regenerates for free.

qa.q: What does a Raft leader failover look like to a client?
qa.a: Writes stall for the election timeout (typically a few hundred ms to a couple of seconds), the new leader is elected with all committed entries, and clients retry with the same idempotency keys. No committed write is lost.

concepts.name: CAP and PACELC: dispatch vs payments
concepts.explain: CAP says that when a network partition happens, a distributed system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write, as if there were one copy) and availability (every request to a non-failed node gets a response). Partitions are not optional in real networks, so the practical question is what each component does during one. PACELC extends this: if Partitioned, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, in normal operation, choose Latency or Consistency, because even without failures, stronger consistency requires coordination round trips. Dynamo and Cassandra are PA/EL; Spanner and etcd are PC/EC; many systems are mixed. The senior insight is that CAP is a per-operation, per-data-type choice, not a property of a whole product. The cost of inconsistency differs wildly: showing a car icon 20 metres off is harmless, while two drivers sent to one rider wastes a driver, and two charges for one trip is a regulatory and trust incident. Good designs make the boundary explicit, keep the AP side rebuildable and the CP side small, and ensure the AP side never makes an irreversible decision without passing through the CP side.
concepts.in_this_design: Location ingestion, nearby cars, candidate search, surge reads and ETAs are PA/EL: keep serving possibly stale data during partitions, and prefer low latency in normal operation. Driver leases, trip state transitions and the ledger are PC/EC: refuse or delay writes rather than diverge. The matcher is AP for finding candidates and CP at the moment it commits an assignment.
key_points: CAP is chosen per operation, not per system.
PACELC: even without partitions, consistency costs latency.
Dispatch discovery is PA/EL; driver lease, trip and money are PC/EC.
Irreversible decisions must pass through the CP side.
Keep the CP surface small so its latency and availability cost stays contained.

qa.q: Is Uber AP or CP?
qa.a: Neither as a whole. Location and discovery are AP because stale data is cheap and availability matters most; assignment, trip state and payments are CP because divergence there costs money and trust.

qa.q: During a partition, what does the rider see?
qa.a: If the rider's region and its lease store are reachable, everything works. If the matcher cannot reach the lease store, it cannot assign, so the rider waits and retries; the app still shows nearby cars from the AP side. We trade matching availability for no double assignment.

qa.q: Where does PACELC 'else latency' show up in this design?
qa.a: A synchronous cross-region ledger commit adds 50-150 ms to every capture. We accept that for money because captures are off the rider's critical path, but we would never put it on the location write path.

qa.q: Could surge be CP?
qa.a: It could, but there is no benefit. Surge is an estimate; staleness of a minute is fine. The rider is protected by the signed quote, which is what makes the charged price consistent.

concepts.name: Matching and dispatch algorithms (greedy, batched, bipartite)
concepts.explain: Matching pairs requests with drivers to optimise an objective such as total pickup time, completion probability or driver earnings. Greedy matching serves each request on arrival with the best currently available driver; it has the lowest latency and is simple, but it is myopic: an early request can take the only driver who is close to a later request. Batched matching collects requests and drivers over a short window (one to a few seconds) and solves an assignment problem on the bipartite graph of requests and drivers, where edge weights are costs such as ETA. The Hungarian algorithm solves the min-cost perfect assignment in O(n^3); for hundreds of nodes per zone this is milliseconds. For larger or sparse graphs, auction algorithms, min-cost max-flow, or greedy approximations with local improvement are used. Real dispatch adds constraints and soft costs: vehicle type, driver destination filters, predicted acceptance probability, rider and driver ratings, dead-head distance after drop-off, fairness among drivers, and for pooled rides, route insertion with detour limits. Advanced systems also look ahead: match a driver who will finish a trip nearby in 2 minutes instead of an idle driver 8 minutes away, and revise plans as new information arrives. The window size is a trade-off between solution quality and added latency.
concepts.in_this_design: Uber's DISCO matches demand to supply using the geo index for candidates and road ETAs for ranking, and can plan into the future (e.g. assign a driver about to drop off nearby). Our design uses greedy nearest-ETA in sparse areas, and in dense zones a 1-2 s batch per zone with a min-cost assignment over costs = ETA + penalties; every chosen pair still goes through the lease CAS before the offer.
key_points: Greedy: lowest latency, myopic. Batched: better global outcome, adds a window of latency.
Bipartite min-cost assignment: Hungarian O(n^3), auction or min-cost flow at larger scale.
Rank by road ETA, not straight-line distance; a river or one-way street changes everything.
Include future supply (drivers finishing nearby) and acceptance probability in costs.
The optimiser proposes; the lease store disposes.

qa.q: Give a concrete example where batching beats greedy.
qa.a: Rider A arrives first: driver X is 1 minute away, Y is 2. Rider B arrives 300 ms later: X is 1 minute away, Y is 10. Greedy gives A X and B Y for 11 minutes total; batching gives A Y and B X for 3 minutes total.

qa.q: How do you pick the batch window?
qa.a: Measure: it must be short enough that it is invisible relative to the offer and acceptance time (2 s is small next to a 15 s accept window) and long enough to collect competing requests in dense zones. Make it adaptive per zone by request rate.

qa.q: What if the chosen driver declines?
qa.a: Release the lease, mark the pair as excluded, and put the request back into the next batch or greedy round with a priority boost for waiting time, so riders who waited longer do not keep losing.

qa.q: Hungarian is O(n^3). What if a zone has 5,000 requests and 10,000 drivers?
qa.a: Sparsify: only connect each request to its top-K nearest drivers by ETA, giving a sparse graph that min-cost flow or an auction algorithm solves quickly. Also split the zone into subzones with overlap margins.

concepts.name: ETA and routing (Dijkstra, A*, contraction hierarchies, traffic)
concepts.explain: A road network is a weighted directed graph: intersections are nodes, road segments are edges, weights are travel times. Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths by settling nodes in order of distance using a priority queue, O(E + V log V); on a country-sized graph with tens of millions of nodes a long query settles millions of nodes and takes seconds. A* adds a heuristic (straight-line distance divided by maximum speed) that never overestimates, steering the search toward the target; it helps but still explores widely. Bidirectional search runs from both ends and meets in the middle. Contraction hierarchies (CH) preprocess the graph: nodes are ordered by importance and contracted one by one, adding shortcut edges whenever removing a node would lengthen a shortest path. A query then runs bidirectional Dijkstra that only relaxes edges toward more important nodes, settling a few hundred nodes, so queries take around a millisecond and many-to-many tables are cheap. The catch is that preprocessing assumes fixed weights. Traffic changes weights constantly, so production systems use customizable approaches (CCH, Customizable Route Planning with multilevel partitions) where topology preprocessing is done once and the metric customisation for new traffic weights takes seconds. Live traffic itself is estimated from probe data: map-matched GPS traces give segment speeds. Finally, route-based ETAs have systematic errors (pickup time, signals, parking), which ML models correct.
concepts.in_this_design: Dispatch needs ETAs from up to 20 candidate drivers to each pickup (many-to-one), about 60k queries per second at peak, plus quotes. The routing engine runs CH-style queries on a graph with traffic weights derived from the driver ping stream, and a DeepETA-style model predicts the residual between routing ETA and actual arrival, as Uber describes.
key_points: Dijkstra settles nodes in distance order; too slow for country-scale at high QPS.
A* uses an admissible heuristic to focus the search.
Contraction hierarchies: preprocess with shortcuts, query upward-only, about 1 ms.
Traffic needs customizable variants (CCH/CRP) so weights update in seconds.
Route ETA plus ML residual beats either alone.

qa.q: Why not just use haversine distance for ranking drivers?
qa.a: Straight-line distance ignores rivers, one-way streets, flyovers and U-turns. A driver 300 m away across a highway may be 8 minutes away by road. Ranking on haversine causes long pickups and cancellations; it is a fallback only.

qa.q: How do contraction hierarchies cope with traffic?
qa.a: Plain CH must be rebuilt when weights change, which takes minutes. Customizable CH keeps the node ordering and shortcut structure from topology alone and recomputes shortcut weights for the new metric in seconds, so traffic can be refreshed every minute or so.

qa.q: Where does live traffic come from?
qa.a: From our own drivers: map-matched ping trails give observed speeds per road segment, aggregated in streaming windows and blended with historical speed profiles by hour of week.

qa.q: Why add ML on top of routing?
qa.a: Routing ETA misses things like time to find the rider, parking, turn penalties and local patterns. Learning the residual keeps the physical model's generalisation and fixes its systematic biases; Uber's DeepETA is exactly this.

concepts.name: Dynamic pricing with streaming aggregation (windows, watermarks)
concepts.explain: Stream processing computes results continuously over unbounded event streams. Aggregations need windows: tumbling windows are fixed, non-overlapping buckets (every minute); sliding or hopping windows overlap (5 minutes long, every 30 s); session windows close after inactivity. Events carry an event time (when it happened on the device) and arrive at processing time, which can be later and out of order, especially from mobile clients. Watermarks are the processor's estimate that no events older than time T are still coming; a window fires when the watermark passes its end, and allowed lateness keeps the window open a little longer for stragglers. Stateful processors such as Flink keep per-key state (counts per cell), checkpoint it consistently with the input offsets, and restore on failure for exactly-once state updates. Dynamic pricing uses such aggregates: demand (requests, app opens) and supply (available drivers) per area per window feed a function that raises price when demand exceeds supply, both to ration rides and to attract more drivers. Good pricing systems smooth over space and time to avoid flicker, cap increases, and predict short-term demand rather than only reacting.
concepts.in_this_design: A Flink job reads requests, app opens and driver locations from the aggregate Kafka cluster, keys by H3 res-8 cell, uses 1-minute windows with about 10 s allowed lateness, smooths across kRing neighbours and with an EWMA, applies city caps, and writes multipliers with a TTL to a KV store. As Uber's real-time infrastructure paper describes, each region computes surge in Flink from aggregate Kafka, but only the primary region writes, and freshness is favoured over consistency.
key_points: Tumbling, sliding and session windows answer different questions.
Event time + watermarks handle out-of-order mobile data; allowed lateness trades accuracy for delay.
Checkpointed state gives exactly-once state inside the processor.
Smooth over space and time, cap, and lock the price in a signed quote.
Surge is an estimate: freshness and availability over consistency.

qa.q: Why not compute surge with a SQL query every minute?
qa.a: At hundreds of thousands of events per second, re-scanning a table each minute is expensive and late; a streaming job keeps running counts per cell and emits results the moment a window closes.

qa.q: Events from drivers in tunnels arrive 2 minutes late. Does surge care?
