qa.a: Mostly no. Allowed lateness is short (about 10 s); very late events are dropped from the live computation and only affect offline analytics. The cost of waiting for them would be stale prices for everyone.

qa.q: How do you run surge across regions?
qa.a: Every region's Flink job consumes the same aggregate Kafka stream and computes the same result, but a coordinator designates one primary writer. On region failure, another region is promoted; its state is already warm because it was computing all along.

qa.q: How do you stop riders gaming surge by moving one block?
qa.a: Spatial smoothing across neighbouring hexagons makes adjacent cells similar, and multipliers change at most a bounded amount per minute.

concepts.name: Event streaming, exactly-once vs at-least-once, and idempotency
concepts.explain: Message delivery has three guarantees. At-most-once: send and forget; messages can be lost. At-least-once: retry until acknowledged; nothing is lost, but duplicates happen whenever an ack is lost after processing. Exactly-once delivery over an unreliable network is impossible in general (the two generals problem), but exactly-once effect is achievable: deliver at least once and make processing idempotent, so applying a message twice has the same result as once. Kafka offers an idempotent producer (sequence numbers per partition so broker-side retries do not duplicate) and transactions that atomically write output records and consumer offsets, giving exactly-once semantics for read-process-write pipelines that stay inside Kafka. Once a side effect leaves Kafka, such as charging a card or sending an SMS, Kafka transactions cannot help; you need idempotency at the destination, usually a unique key stored with the result. Natural keys (trip_id + operation) are better than random UUIDs because a retry that re-derives the key gets the same one. Ordering is per partition, so partition by the entity whose events must stay ordered (driver_id, trip_id). The transactional outbox pattern avoids the dual-write problem: write the state change and the event to the same database transaction, and a relay publishes the event afterwards.
concepts.in_this_design: Kafka carries pings (partition by driver_id), trip events (partition by trip_id) and payment events. Trip service writes an outbox row in the same Docstore transaction as each state change. Consumers are at-least-once and idempotent: payments key on capture:{trip_id}, notifications on event_id, ratings on (trip_id, role). Flink uses checkpointed exactly-once state for surge. Uber replicates Kafka across regions with uReplicator into aggregate clusters.
key_points: Exactly-once delivery is impossible; exactly-once effect = at-least-once + idempotency.
Kafka EOS covers Kafka-to-Kafka pipelines, not external side effects.
Use deterministic natural keys so retries reproduce the same idempotency key.
Partition by the entity whose order matters.
Outbox pattern: state and event in one transaction, relay publishes later.

qa.q: Kafka has exactly-once semantics. Why do you still need idempotency?
qa.a: Kafka transactions make a consume-transform-produce loop atomic within Kafka. Calling a PSP or sending a push happens outside that transaction, so a crash after the call but before the offset commit replays the message; only an idempotency key at the PSP and our payments DB prevents a second charge.

qa.q: What is the dual-write problem?
qa.a: Updating the database and publishing to Kafka as two separate steps means a crash between them leaves them inconsistent: state changed but no event, or an event for a change that rolled back. The outbox pattern or change data capture fixes it.

qa.q: How do you keep events for one trip in order?
qa.a: Key the topic by trip_id so all events for a trip land in one partition, include a version number, and have consumers ignore versions older than what they have applied.

qa.q: Random UUID or natural idempotency key?
qa.a: Natural keys like capture:{trip_id} are deterministic: any retry from any service derives the same key. A random UUID generated per attempt defeats the purpose unless it is persisted before the first attempt.

concepts.name: Saga and distributed transactions (trip + payment)
concepts.explain: A distributed transaction changes state in several services or databases that cannot share one local transaction. Two-phase commit (2PC) uses a coordinator: prepare all participants (each locks and promises it can commit), then commit all. It gives atomicity but blocks if the coordinator fails between phases, holds locks for the duration, and requires every participant to support prepare, which external payment processors do not. A saga breaks the business transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action that semantically undoes it (void an authorisation, refund a capture, release a driver). If step 3 fails, compensations for steps 2 and 1 run. Sagas give eventual consistency, not isolation: intermediate states are visible, so the design must make them safe (e.g. 'payment pending'). Sagas can be choreographed (services react to each other's events) or orchestrated (a central workflow tells each service what to do and records progress). Orchestration is easier to reason about and monitor for long, money-moving flows; durable workflow engines such as Uber's Cadence (and its fork Temporal) persist each step so the saga resumes after crashes. Every step must be idempotent because the orchestrator will retry.
concepts.in_this_design: The ride saga: create trip and authorise the estimated fare (compensation: void auth), match and reserve driver (compensation: release lease, void auth if rider cancels), complete trip and capture final fare with incremental auth if needed (compensation: refund), write ledger entries and schedule driver payout. A Cadence-style workflow orchestrates it with idempotency keys on every PSP call; Uber's Gulfstream uses immutable orders with deterministic ids and double-entry ledger entries that sum to zero.
key_points: 2PC blocks and needs every participant to cooperate; PSPs will not.
Saga = local transactions + compensating actions; eventual, not isolated.
Orchestration (durable workflow) beats choreography for money flows.
Every step and compensation must be idempotent and retryable.
Design intermediate states to be visible and safe.

qa.q: The capture fails after the trip ended. What happens?
qa.a: The workflow retries with backoff and the same key; if the card is declined, it tries the backup payment method, and failing that records an outstanding balance on the rider's account and blocks new requests until settled. The driver is still paid from the ledger.

qa.q: Why is auth-then-capture a natural saga?
qa.a: Authorisation reserves funds without moving money, so its compensation (void) is cheap and free. Capture happens only after the service is delivered, when the final amount is known.

qa.q: Choreography or orchestration for this flow?
qa.a: Orchestration: there are many steps, timeouts and branches (cancel fees, tips, disputes), and finance needs to see the state of every saga. Choreography is fine for side effects like notifications.

qa.q: What about isolation problems in sagas?
qa.a: Use semantic locks and state: the trip shows 'payment pending' and the rider cannot start a new trip while an unpaid balance exists; commutative ledger entries avoid lost updates.

concepts.name: Real-time push (WebSockets, long polling, SSE, MQTT, mobile push)
concepts.explain: Servers need to tell clients things the client did not ask for at that moment: a new offer, the driver's position, a cancellation. Short polling (ask every N seconds) is simple but wastes requests and adds up to N seconds of delay. Long polling holds the request open until there is data or a timeout, then the client reconnects; it works through almost any proxy but costs a request per message. Server-sent events stream one-way over HTTP. WebSockets upgrade an HTTP connection to a full-duplex, framed channel with low per-message overhead, ideal for both streaming pings up and offers down. MQTT is a lightweight publish-subscribe protocol designed for unreliable networks, with small headers, keepalives, quality-of-service levels (0 at most once, 1 at least once, 2 exactly once between client and broker) and session resumption; it suits mobile devices on 2G/3G. When the app is backgrounded or killed, the OS closes sockets, so platform push (APNs, FCM) wakes it, with no delivery-time guarantee. Persistent connections create a routing problem: the service that wants to notify a user must know which gateway node holds that user's connection, which calls for a connection registry, plus heartbeats, reconnection with jittered backoff and resynchronisation of missed state.
concepts.in_this_design: Drivers and riders keep one persistent connection (WebSocket or MQTT-style) to an edge gateway; pings flow up, offers and live driver positions flow down. A connection registry maps user -> gateway node with a 60 s TTL. Critical messages fall back to APNs/FCM and then SMS. On reconnect, the client calls GET /trips/{id} to resync and then receives deltas. 8M concurrent connections at about 50k per node means roughly 160 gateway nodes plus headroom.
key_points: Polling wastes requests; long polling is the universal fallback; WebSocket/MQTT for real time.
MQTT is built for lossy mobile networks: tiny headers, keepalive, QoS, session resume.
Platform push wakes backgrounded apps but has no latency guarantee.
A connection registry routes server-initiated messages to the right gateway.
Always resync state after reconnect; deltas alone are not enough.

qa.q: Why not use FCM/APNs for driver offers?
qa.a: They are best-effort with no latency SLO, can be throttled or delayed by the OS, and the offer window is 15 s. The foreground app uses its own socket; platform push is only the fallback to wake the app.

qa.q: How do you scale to millions of WebSocket connections?
qa.a: Gateways are mostly idle memory per connection (tens of KB), so tune file descriptors and kernel buffers to hold about 50k-100k per node, keep them stateless apart from the connection, store routing in a registry, and drain gracefully on deploy with staggered reconnects.

qa.q: What happens to messages sent while a client is reconnecting?
qa.a: They are not reliably delivered over the socket. Important state is pulled by the client on reconnect (resync endpoint), offers still valid are re-sent, and critical alerts go via push and SMS.

qa.q: When would you choose long polling?
qa.a: When corporate proxies or old networks block WebSocket upgrades. It is a good fallback the client can switch to automatically.

concepts.name: Rate limiting
concepts.explain: Rate limiting caps how often a client can perform an action, protecting the system from abuse, bugs and overload, and keeping one tenant from starving others. Token bucket: a bucket holds up to B tokens and refills at R per second; each request takes a token; it allows bursts up to B and an average of R. Leaky bucket: requests drain at a constant rate from a queue, smoothing bursts. Fixed window counters are cheap but allow double bursts at window edges; sliding window log is exact but stores every timestamp; sliding window counter interpolates between two fixed windows and is a good compromise. In a distributed system, a global limit needs shared state (Redis with atomic Lua scripts) or approximate local limits per node that sync periodically. Limits are applied at several layers: at the edge per IP and device, per authenticated user and endpoint, and internally per caller service. Beyond static limits, adaptive concurrency limits (based on observed latency, like TCP congestion control) and priority-based load shedding protect services under unexpected load. Responses should say how long to wait (429 with Retry-After) so well-behaved clients back off.
concepts.in_this_design: Gateways enforce per-driver ping limits (about 2/s), per-rider quote and request limits, per-device signup and login limits (against account farming and credential stuffing), and promo-code attempt limits. Internally, ETA and matching services use adaptive concurrency limits and shed low-priority callers (nearby cars) before dispatch.
key_points: Token bucket allows bursts and an average rate; the common default.
Sliding window counter is the cheap, accurate-enough choice for per-user limits.
Local limits with periodic sync scale better than a central counter on every request.
Layer limits: IP/device at edge, user per endpoint, service-to-service internally.
Prefer priority shedding over uniform rejection under overload.

qa.q: Why rate limit driver pings if you control the app?
qa.a: Bugs, modified clients and spoofing tools exist. A single buggy app release sending 10 pings per second would multiply ingest load. A limit protects the shared index and flags abnormal clients.

qa.q: Central Redis counter or local limits?
qa.a: A central counter is exact but adds a network hop per request and is a hot dependency. For most per-user limits, a local token bucket on the gateway with sticky routing, or local counters synced every few hundred milliseconds, is accurate enough and far cheaper.

qa.q: How do you rate limit internally during a city spike?
qa.a: Assign priorities: dispatch ETAs above quote ETAs above nearby-car ETAs, and use adaptive concurrency limits so when latency rises the service admits fewer low-priority requests.

qa.q: Fixed window problem?
qa.a: With 100 per minute, a client can send 100 at 0:59 and 100 at 1:00, 200 in two seconds. Sliding windows or token buckets avoid that.

concepts.name: Leader election, distributed locks and fencing (no double-assigned driver)
concepts.explain: Some decisions must be made by exactly one actor at a time: one node should own a partition, one matcher should assign a driver. Leader election picks such an actor, typically using a consensus service (ZooKeeper ephemeral sequential nodes, etcd leases, Raft itself) so that the choice survives failures. A distributed lock is the same idea scoped to a resource. The trap is that a lock holder can pause (garbage collection, network delay) past its lease expiry, a new holder is granted the lock, and the old one wakes up and writes anyway: two writers. Leases bound how long a crashed holder blocks others, but they cannot stop a paused holder. The fix is fencing tokens: every grant comes with a monotonically increasing number, and the resource (storage) rejects writes carrying a token lower than the highest it has seen. Locks built on asynchronous replication or quorum-less caches (single Redis, or Redlock with clock assumptions) are unsafe for correctness; use them only for efficiency (avoiding duplicate work). For correctness, either use a linearizable store with compare-and-set and fencing, or avoid locks entirely by giving each resource a single owner that serialises operations.
concepts.in_this_design: Assigning a driver is a conditional write on the driver state row in a linearizable store: CAS AVAILABLE -> OFFERED with a 15 s lease and a new fencing token. Accept and start must present the current token. The surge writer and the outbox relay per partition are elected leaders (one writer). Ringpop ownership is only an efficiency hint, never the lock.
key_points: Leases bound crash blocking; fencing tokens stop paused holders.
Locks for efficiency can be sloppy; locks for correctness need consensus plus fencing.
Prefer CAS on the resource itself to an external lock service.
Single-owner serialisation is often simpler than locking.
Never trust wall clocks for mutual exclusion.

qa.q: Why not use a Redis SETNX lock to reserve a driver?
qa.a: A single Redis node can fail over to a replica that never received the lock, and a paused client can outlive its TTL. Two matchers could then both believe they hold the driver. Use a consensus-backed store with CAS and fencing, so the write itself is the lock.

qa.q: Explain fencing tokens with a concrete failure.
qa.a: Matcher A reserves driver D with token 41, then stalls in a GC pause. The lease expires; matcher B reserves D with token 42 and sends an offer, which D accepts. A wakes and tries to confirm with token 41; the store rejects it because 42 is current. Without the token, A would overwrite B's assignment.

qa.q: Where do you need leader election in this design?
qa.a: Single writer for surge output per region pair, one outbox relay per partition, Raft leaders inside each Docstore partition, and the control plane that decides city failover.

qa.q: Is a 15 s lease too long?
qa.a: It matches the driver's decision window. If the driver app is dead, the rider waits up to 15 s before re-dispatch; we shorten that by releasing early on explicit decline and by not offering to drivers whose last ping is stale.

concepts.name: Multi-region active-active and failover
concepts.explain: Running in multiple regions protects against the loss of a whole datacenter or cloud region and puts compute near users. Active-passive keeps a standby that takes over on failure; it is simpler but the standby is cold-ish, failover is rarely exercised and capacity sits idle. Active-active serves traffic from every region at once; it is efficient and always tested, but concurrent writes to the same data in two regions cause conflicts unless each key has a single home (write locality) or the data type merges automatically (CRDTs). The practical pattern is partitioned active-active: every region is live, but each partition (a city, a user) is homed in one region at a time, with replicas elsewhere ready to be promoted. Failover then involves detecting the failure, deciding (ideally automated with human override), moving traffic (DNS with low TTL, anycast, client-side region lists), promoting data, and rebuilding soft state. RPO (data loss) and RTO (downtime) targets drive the replication mode. Failover must be drilled regularly, capacity in the surviving regions must cover the extra load, and failback must be planned too, since it is often harder than failover.
concepts.in_this_design: Each city is homed in one region (active), with a designated standby; all regions serve traffic for their own cities. Trips replicate asynchronously (RPO under a second) with the driver-held encrypted trip digest as backstop, as Uber described; the ledger replicates synchronously. Kafka uses regional plus aggregate clusters; surge runs active-active compute with a single primary writer; consumers like payments run active-passive with offset sync.
key_points: Active-active with per-partition homing avoids write conflicts.
Soft state (geo index) rebuilds itself; replicate only what cannot be rebuilt.
RPO and RTO per data type decide sync vs async replication.
Keep N+1 regional capacity or failover causes a second outage.
Drill failover and failback; untested failover does not exist.

qa.q: Why not let both regions accept writes for the same trip?
qa.a: Two regions could apply conflicting transitions (cancel in one, start in the other) and there is no meaningful merge. Homing each trip to one region keeps transitions serialised; the other region only takes over after explicit failover.

qa.q: How does the driver phone help in failover?
qa.a: Dispatch periodically gives the driver app an encrypted digest of the trip state. If the new region does not know the trip because replication lagged, the next ping reveals an unknown trip and the app uploads the digest, letting the server restore it without synchronous cross-region replication.

qa.q: What capacity do you keep for failover?
qa.a: Enough that losing the largest region still leaves surviving regions under about 80% utilisation at peak; with three regions that means running each at roughly 50-60% normally.

qa.q: How do you avoid split-brain during failover?
qa.a: The control plane that re-homes cities is itself consensus-backed, the old region's writes are fenced (epoch number per city home), and stale writes with an old epoch are rejected.

concepts.name: Trip lifecycle state machine and optimistic concurrency
concepts.explain: Business entities that move through stages are best modelled as explicit finite state machines: a fixed set of states, a table of allowed transitions, and guards on each. This makes illegal states unrepresentable (a trip cannot be COMPLETED before ON_TRIP), centralises business rules, and makes auditing simple because every change is a named event. In a distributed system several actors may try to move the same entity concurrently: the rider cancels while the driver starts, a retry arrives after the original succeeded. Pessimistic locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE) serialises them but holds locks across network calls. Optimistic concurrency control instead reads the entity with its version, computes the change, and writes only if the version is unchanged (compare-and-set); the loser gets a conflict and re-reads. It is ideal when conflicts are rare but must be handled correctly. Idempotency fits naturally: store the last applied event id so a retried event returns the current state instead of failing. Every transition should also emit an event (via an outbox) so other services react, and the history of transitions becomes the audit log support teams need.
concepts.in_this_design: Trip states: REQUESTED -> MATCHED -> ARRIVED -> ON_TRIP -> COMPLETED, with CANCELLED from REQUESTED, MATCHED or ARRIVED and EXPIRED from REQUESTED. Each API call carries expected_version; Docstore applies a conditional update and inserts an outbox event in the same transaction. Driver state (OFFLINE, AVAILABLE, OFFERED, EN_ROUTE, ON_TRIP) is a second state machine kept consistent with the trip via the fencing token.
key_points: Explicit state machines make illegal transitions impossible and audits trivial.
Optimistic concurrency: read version, write if unchanged, loser re-reads.
Store last event id for idempotent replays.
Emit every transition through an outbox for downstream consumers.
Keep the driver and trip state machines linked by the lease token.

qa.q: Rider cancel and driver start arrive together. Walk me through it.
qa.a: Both read version 7. Start commits first and sets version 8, ON_TRIP. Cancel's conditional update with version 7 fails, returns 409 with the current state; the rider app shows the trip has started and offers to end it or contact support.

qa.q: Why not use SELECT FOR UPDATE?
qa.a: It holds row locks while the request does other work and can deadlock across tables. With conflicts rare, optimistic CAS gives the same correctness with no lock waits.

qa.q: How do you make transitions idempotent?
qa.a: Each client event carries an id; the trip row stores the last applied event id (or a small set). A retry with the same id returns the current trip with 200 rather than a conflict.

qa.q: What if the driver app thinks the trip ended but the server never got it?
qa.a: The app keeps the END event queued with its id and resends on reconnect; the server applies it once. Fare uses the server's map-matched trail up to the end timestamp, so the delay does not change the price.

tradeoffs.options: Geohash strings, quadtree, S2 cells, H3 hexagons, PostGIS R-tree
tradeoffs.choice: H3 cells (res 8-9) as keys in an in-memory hash map
tradeoffs.why: O(1) updates for 1.25M writes/s, uniform neighbour distance for kRing search and surge smoothing, integer ids as shard keys. Quadtree adapts to density but rebalancing under constant movement is costly; R-trees are great for ad hoc polygons but slow to update at this rate.

tradeoffs.decision: Greedy nearest vs batched global matching
tradeoffs.options: Offer nearest driver immediately; batch requests for 1-2 s and solve assignment
tradeoffs.choice: Greedy in sparse areas, batched in dense zones and airports
tradeoffs.why: Batching lowers total pickup time and improves fairness but adds up to 2 s of latency; it pays off only when several requests compete for the same drivers.

tradeoffs.options: Database rows, Redis GEO, custom in-memory sharded index
tradeoffs.choice: Custom in-memory index on a Ringpop ring with Kafka for durability
tradeoffs.why: Latest position is overwrite-only and rebuildable in 4 s, so durability on the hot path is wasted cost; Kafka keeps the history for everything else.

tradeoffs.choice: AP for location and candidate search; CP for driver lease, trip state and money
tradeoffs.why: Stale locations cost a few metres; a double-assigned driver or double charge costs trust and money. Pay the latency of consensus only where correctness needs it.

tradeoffs.decision: Shard key for the real-time plane
tradeoffs.choice: City first, then H3 parent cell within the city
tradeoffs.why: Queries are spatial so spatial sharding keeps a kRing on one or two shards; city isolation gives blast-radius control and region homing. Cost: hot cells, solved by splitting and read replicas.

tradeoffs.options: Polling, long polling, WebSocket, MQTT, platform push only
tradeoffs.choice: Persistent WebSocket/MQTT-style connection with APNs/FCM fallback and SMS for critical
tradeoffs.why: Offers have a 15 s window and live tracking needs ~2 s freshness; platform push alone has no delivery guarantee or latency SLO.

tradeoffs.options: Charge upfront, authorise then capture, charge after trip only
tradeoffs.choice: Authorise estimate at request, capture final at completion
tradeoffs.why: Auth proves funds before a driver drives to you; capture after lets the fare change; void on cancel is free. Charging only after the trip risks unpaid trips.

tradeoffs.decision: Distributed transaction across trip and payment
tradeoffs.options: 2PC across services, saga with compensations, single shared DB
tradeoffs.choice: Orchestrated saga (Cadence) with idempotent steps and outbox events
tradeoffs.why: PSPs cannot participate in 2PC and holding locks across a 3 s network call is fragile; a saga with compensations (void, refund) matches how money really moves.

tradeoffs.options: Active-passive whole site, active-active with global writes, cities homed to a region with standby
tradeoffs.choice: Each city active in one home region, warm standby in another; global services active-active with single writer per key
tradeoffs.why: Dispatch is local by nature, so homing avoids cross-region write conflicts while still giving every region live traffic; failover is per city, limiting blast radius.

tradeoffs.options: Per city, per geohash, per H3 res-7/8/9, per road segment
tradeoffs.choice: H3 res-8 (~0.7 km^2) with neighbour smoothing, 1 minute windows
tradeoffs.why: Small enough to reflect local imbalance, large enough for statistically meaningful counts; smoothing prevents riders walking 100 m to escape surge.

tradeoffs.options: Haversine x factor, Dijkstra/A*, contraction hierarchies, ML only
tradeoffs.choice: CH (customizable for traffic) plus ML residual
tradeoffs.why: CH gives ms queries for dispatch volume; ML fixes systematic errors like pickup time and signals; haversine is a degradation fallback only.

tradeoffs.options: At-most-once, at-least-once + idempotent consumers, Kafka transactions EOS
tradeoffs.choice: At-least-once with idempotent consumers; Flink checkpoint EOS inside the surge job
tradeoffs.why: End-to-end exactly-once across PSPs is impossible; idempotency at the effect is the only real guarantee, and it is cheap with natural keys like trip_id.

failure_modes.behavior: Control plane re-homes affected cities to the standby region; GeoDNS and client failover lists move connections within ~1 minute; geo index rebuilds from the next pings; trips come from the replicated store or driver-held digests; payments replay idempotently from replicated Kafka/outbox. New requests may fail for 1-3 minutes; in-progress trips continue on the phones.

failure_modes.failure: Matching service (DISCO) down in one city
failure_modes.behavior: Requests queue in Demand service for up to 30 s with a 'finding your ride' UI; a fallback simple greedy matcher (nearest AVAILABLE by haversine with lease) can be enabled by flag; if both are down, return a clear error rather than holding riders indefinitely. Active trips are unaffected because they no longer depend on dispatch.

SWIM marks it suspect then faulty in a few seconds; ring ownership of its cells moves to neighbours; the follower replica is promoted or the new owner fills from the next pings within 4 s. Dispatch in those cells sees fewer candidates for a few seconds.

failure_modes.failure: Kafka cluster in a region degraded
failure_modes.behavior: Hot path is unaffected because pings update the index synchronously and Kafka is async; producers buffer then fail over to another regional cluster; surge uses last known values with TTL decay; payments outbox keeps events in the DB until Kafka recovers, so nothing is lost.

Circuit breaker opens on the PSP; new trips proceed with deferred auth for low-risk riders (risk-scored), captures queue in the saga and retry with jittered backoff and the same keys; failover to secondary PSP for new auths.

Bulkheaded pools: dispatch ETAs prioritised over quote and nearby-car ETAs; quote ETA degrades to cached cell-to-cell ETA tables, then haversine x city speed factor; load shedding on low-priority callers.

failure_modes.failure: Network partition between matcher and lease store
failure_modes.behavior: Matcher cannot reserve, so it cannot offer; requests wait/retry. This is the deliberate CP choice: we lose availability of matching in that partition rather than risk double assignment.

Plausibility checks drop teleports; map matching snaps to roads; fare recomputed from the matched trail; repeated anomalies flag the account; dispatch ignores drivers with stale or low-accuracy positions.

Trip stays ON_TRIP server-side; the app buffers events and pings; rider's map shows last known position and 'updating'; on reconnect buffered data is merged in seq order; if the driver never reconnects, support tooling ends the trip using the last known point and the route.

Clients reconnect with jittered backoff to other nodes; connection registry entries expire (TTL 60 s) or are overwritten on reconnect; pushes during the gap fall back to APNs/FCM; offers re-sent on reconnect if still valid.

failure_modes.failure: Surge job produces a bad multiplier (bug, bad data)
failure_modes.behavior: Guard rails: per-city caps, max delta per minute, anomaly detection on output distribution, kill switch to 1.0x; quotes are signed with the multiplier so riders are charged what they saw.
Correctness never depends on wall clocks: ordering uses versions, sequence numbers and fencing tokens; leases are checked by the store's clock only.

metrics: Request-to-offer latency p50/p95/p99 per city (SLO p95 < 2 s).
Offer acceptance rate and time-to-accept; re-dispatch rounds per trip.
Match rate and unfulfilled requests per H3 cell per minute.
Location ingest rate, lag from receive to index (p99 < 1 s), and dropped/invalid ping ratio.
Geo index freshness: share of AVAILABLE drivers with ping older than 15 s.
Double-assignment detector: count of drivers with two active trips (must be 0, page on 1).
ETA error: MAPE and median absolute error for pickup and drop ETAs, by city and hour.
Cancellation rate after match, split by rider and driver, and by pickup ETA bucket.
Surge pipeline end-to-end latency and staleness of KV entries; multiplier distribution.
WebSocket connected ratio, reconnect rate, push delivery latency and fallback rate.
Payments: auth success rate, capture success, PENDING age, duplicate-charge detector, ledger imbalance (must be 0), reconciliation mismatches.
Kafka consumer lag per critical consumer group (payments, surge, fraud).
SWIM membership churn, ring rebalances per hour, shard load skew (max/mean).
Driver utilisation and dead-head kilometres per trip (marketplace health).
Error budget burn rate per region for the request flow.

follow_ups.q: Why not just use Redis GEOADD/GEOSEARCH for driver locations?
follow_ups.a: Redis GEO is a sorted set keyed by a 52-bit geohash, so it is a fine baseline for one city. At 1.25M writes/s globally you still need to shard it, choose a shard key, and handle cross-shard radius queries yourself, and a single hot key per city would melt. Uber's answer was an in-process sharded index with S2, later H3, cell ids; I would start with Redis per city for an MVP and move to a custom index when one city's write rate exceeds a single node's capacity.

follow_ups.q: How do you guarantee a driver is never assigned to two riders?
follow_ups.a: The driver state store is the single source of truth and it is linearizable per driver. Matchers can only offer after a compare-and-set from AVAILABLE to OFFERED succeeds, which also issues a monotonically increasing fencing token and a 15 s lease. Every later step (accept, start) must present the current token. Routing via the ring makes contention rare, but correctness comes from the CAS and token, so even a split-brain matcher cannot double assign.

Geohash cells are rectangles whose neighbours sit at two different distances, and two points a metre apart across a cell boundary can have completely different prefixes, so proximity search must always check 8 neighbours. H3 hexagons have six equidistant neighbours, so kRing approximates a circle, and smoothing (surge, supply) behaves uniformly. Geohash wins on simplicity and prefix range scans in a B-tree. S2 wins on exact hierarchical containment. For movement and smoothing, hexagons are the better fit.

follow_ups.q: What happens if the matching service goes down in Mumbai at 9 am?
follow_ups.a: Active trips continue because they no longer depend on dispatch. New requests are held by Demand service for up to 30 s while the matcher's ring rebalances or a standby instance takes the city shard. If the full matcher stays down, a flag enables a simple greedy fallback matcher that uses the same lease store, so it is still safe. Riders see 'high demand, retrying' rather than a spinner forever. We would page on request-to-offer p95 and match rate for that city within a minute.

follow_ups.q: How would you handle a region going down entirely?
follow_ups.a: Cities are homed to one region with a warm standby. Trip and payment data replicate cross-region; the live geo index does not need to, since it rebuilds from pings in seconds. The control plane re-homes the cities, DNS and client failover lists move connections, drivers' next pings fill the index, and any trip the standby has not seen is recreated from the encrypted digest on the driver's phone, which is what Uber described doing. Payments replay from the replicated log with idempotency keys.

follow_ups.q: Is your system CP or AP?
follow_ups.a: Both, deliberately by component. Location and candidate search are AP: during a partition we keep serving slightly stale positions. Driver leases, trip state and the ledger are CP: during a partition we refuse writes rather than diverge. In PACELC terms the geo plane is PA/EL and the money plane is PC/EC.

follow_ups.q: Greedy matching is simple. Why bother with batching?
follow_ups.a: Greedy assigns the nearest driver to whoever asked first. If rider A is 1 minute from driver X and 2 minutes from Y, and rider B (arriving 200 ms later) is 1 minute from X and 10 minutes from Y, greedy gives total 11 minutes; batching gives 3. In dense cities batching over 1-2 s windows lowers total pickup time and cancellations. In sparse areas there is no competition so we skip the wait.

follow_ups.q: How do you compute ETAs fast enough for dispatch?
follow_ups.a: Contraction hierarchies: preprocess the graph by contracting less important nodes and adding shortcuts, so a query is a bidirectional upward-only Dijkstra settling a few hundred nodes, around a millisecond. Traffic changes weights constantly, so we use a customizable variant that recomputes the metric in seconds without redoing the node order. Then an ML model corrects the residual, as Uber's DeepETA does.

follow_ups.q: How do you make the payment flow exactly-once?
follow_ups.a: You cannot get exactly-once delivery, but you can get exactly-once effect. Every money operation has a deterministic key (auth:{trip}, capture:{trip}), stored with the request hash and result before and after calling the PSP, which also receives the same key. Retries return the stored result. Unknown outcomes stay PENDING and are resolved by querying the PSP, then reconciled daily against settlement files.

follow_ups.q: Why not a 2PC between trip service and payments?
follow_ups.a: The PSP will not join our transaction, 2PC blocks if the coordinator dies, and holding locks across a 3 s card call kills throughput. A saga with compensating actions (void the auth, refund) and an outbox to publish events atomically with state is the standard approach and matches how card networks already work.

follow_ups.q: How do you keep the rider's map smooth when pings arrive every 4 s?
follow_ups.a: On trip we raise the rate to 2 s, and the client animates along the map-matched route polyline between points (dead reckoning with speed and heading). The server pushes the latest point over the open socket; the client interpolates, so it looks continuous without more data.

follow_ups.q: How does surge avoid flicker and gaming?
follow_ups.a: Smooth spatially across the H3 kRing, smooth temporally with an EWMA, limit the change per minute, and lock the price in a signed quote. Drivers see a heatmap, not exact multipliers per cell, and supply features include drivers about to drop off nearby, so a few drivers going offline together has limited effect.

follow_ups.q: What is the role of Ringpop and why not a load balancer?
follow_ups.a: Ringpop embeds a consistent hash ring in each service instance with SWIM gossip membership, so any instance can accept a request and forward it to the key's owner. A plain load balancer spreads requests randomly, which breaks in-memory state locality. The trade-off is that Ringpop is AP: during membership churn two nodes may briefly think they own a key, which is why the lease store, not the ring, guards assignment.

follow_ups.q: How would you shard storage for trips?
follow_ups.a: Trips are accessed by trip_id on the hot path, so hash on trip_id within the city's home region for even load. Rider and driver history are secondary indexes, or a separate table keyed by (rider_id, time) populated from the outbox. Avoid sharding trips by city alone because a big city becomes a hot shard.

follow_ups.q: What about data residency in India or the EU?
follow_ups.a: City-to-region homing already gives us locality. For residency we pin those cities to in-country regions, keep PII and precise trails there, and replicate only aggregated or pseudonymised data globally. The standby region for those cities must also be in-country, which constrains failover options and is a real cost to call out.

follow_ups.q: How would you rate limit this system?
follow_ups.a: At the gateway: per-driver ping limit (2/s), per-rider quote limit (e.g. 30/min) and request limit, per-IP and per-device limits for login and signup, all token buckets kept locally with periodic sync to a shared store. Internally, adaptive concurrency limits and priority shedding protect ETA and matching.

follow_ups.q: What would you do differently for UberPool?
follow_ups.a: Pool turns matching into a vehicle routing problem with insertion: for each request, evaluate inserting pickup and drop into existing routes subject to detour limits. It requires batching, a richer cost function and constant re-planning of en-route vehicles, which is why DISCO was designed to revise plans.

key_points: Split the system into an AP real-time plane (locations, candidates) and a CP transactional plane (driver lease, trip, money); say this in the first two minutes.
Location math: 5M drivers / 4 s = 1.25M writes/s, but the live state is only ~1 GB, so keep it in memory, shard for throughput, and stream history to Kafka.
H3 hexagons give equidistant neighbours, clean kRing search and smoothing; geohash is the simple baseline; S2 and quadtrees are the alternatives you should be able to compare.
Shard the real-time plane by city then cell with consistent hashing and SWIM gossip (Ringpop); accept that ownership can briefly overlap.
No double assignment comes from a CAS lease with a fencing token in a linearizable store, not from routing.
Matching: greedy nearest-ETA in sparse areas, batched bipartite assignment every 1-2 s in dense zones; rank on ETA, not straight-line distance.
ETA: contraction hierarchies (customizable for traffic) for ms queries, plus an ML residual model; haversine only as a degradation fallback.
Surge: Flink windowed aggregation per H3 cell per minute from Kafka, smoothed and capped, single-writer from the primary region, locked into a signed upfront quote.
Payments: authorise at request, capture at completion, saga with void/refund compensations, idempotency keys on every hop, double-entry ledger, daily reconciliation.
Trip state machine with versioned conditional updates and an outbox gives ordered, replayable events without dual writes.
Failure story: geo index rebuilds from pings in seconds; trips survive region loss via replication plus a driver-held digest; degrade surge, ETA and map refresh before dispatch.
Measure request-to-offer p95, match rate, ETA error, double-assignment count (0), ledger imbalance (0) and ingest lag.

quiz.q: 5 million drivers are online and each pings every 4 seconds. Roughly how many location writes per second must the system absorb?
quiz.why: 5,000,000 / 4 = 1.25M per second, close to the ~1M writes/s Uber said its geo index was designed for. 5 million is the tempting answer if you forget to divide by the interval.

quiz.q: Why are H3 hexagons preferred over square grid cells for nearby-driver search and surge smoothing?
options: Hexagons have smaller ids than squares
Hexagons tile the sphere perfectly with no exceptions
All six neighbours of a hexagon are equidistant from its centre
Hexagons perfectly nest inside their parent cells
quiz.why: Equidistant neighbours make k-rings approximate circles and treat all neighbours equally. H3 actually needs 12 pentagons, and its children only approximately nest in parents, so the 'perfect nesting' option describes S2, not H3.

quiz.q: Two points 2 metres apart sit on opposite sides of a geohash cell boundary. What is the practical consequence for a proximity query?
options: They are guaranteed to share the same 6-character prefix
Geohash automatically merges them into one cell at the next precision
The query must also search neighbouring cells, not just the point's own cell
The query must switch to a quadtree for those points
quiz.why: Prefixes can differ completely across a boundary, so correct search always includes neighbours. The 'same prefix' option is the common misconception that shared prefix equals nearness in both directions.

quiz.q: Which statement about Google S2 is most accurate?
options: It uses hexagons on an icosahedron
It is a dynamic tree that splits when a node exceeds capacity
It orders cells along a Hilbert curve on a cube projection, giving 64-bit ids with exact hierarchy
It encodes cells as base-32 strings
quiz.why: S2 projects onto six cube faces and orders cells on a Hilbert curve; children share their parent's id prefix exactly. Hexagons on an icosahedron is H3; base-32 strings is geohash.

quiz.q: Why is a quadtree a poor fit for the live driver index compared with a fixed cell grid?
options: Quadtrees only work for one-dimensional data
Constantly moving points force frequent node splits and merges under heavy write load
quiz.why: Quadtrees adapt to density but structural changes under 1M+ moves per second are costly and need locking. They can answer range queries fine, so the first option is wrong.

quiz.q: The location service is falling behind during a spike. Which response is best?
options: Queue all pings durably and process them in order later
Write every ping synchronously to the database to avoid losing any
Collapse queued pings to the newest per driver and raise the ping interval remotely
Reject all pings from the busiest city until the backlog clears
quiz.why: A location is superseded by the next one, so old pings have no value; keep the newest and shed rate. Durable queuing adds lag, so drivers appear where they were minutes ago.

quiz.q: Approximately how much RAM does the latest position of 5 million drivers need at about 200 bytes each?
quiz.why: 5M x 200 B = 1 GB. Sharding the geo index is for write throughput and blast radius, not size. Guessing 100 GB is the usual over-estimate that leads people to put it on disk.

quiz.q: In consistent hashing with virtual nodes, what happens when one of 100 nodes fails?
options: About 50% of keys move to the next node
About 1% of keys move, spread across many surviving nodes
No keys move until an operator rebalances
quiz.why: Only the failed node's keys move, about 1/N, and virtual nodes spread them across many successors. 'All keys remapped' describes hash mod N.

quiz.q: Ringpop routes all reservations for a driver's cell to one owner. Why is a separate CAS lease store still needed?
options: Gossip-based membership is eventually consistent, so two nodes may briefly both think they own a key
Ringpop cannot route requests across machines
The lease store is faster than the ring
Ringpop only works for stateless services
quiz.why: Ring views converge eventually; during churn ownership can overlap. Correctness must come from a linearizable CAS. Ringpop exists precisely to shard stateful services, so the last option is backwards.

quiz.q: In SWIM, what is the purpose of the ping-req (indirect probe) step?
options: To distinguish a dead target from a bad link between the prober and the target
To spread membership updates to all nodes at once
To measure round-trip latency for load balancing
quiz.why: Asking k other members to probe the target uses independent paths, so a lossy link does not cause a false suspicion. Dissemination happens by piggybacking, not by ping-req.

quiz.q: Why does SWIM mark a node 'suspect' before 'faulty'?
options: To reduce the number of pings sent
Because faulty nodes must be confirmed by an operator
To give a slow but alive node a chance to refute with a higher incarnation number
Because suspicion is required by Raft
quiz.why: The suspect state with incarnation-number refutation sharply reduces false positives from GC pauses or slow links. It is not about operators or Raft.

quiz.q: How does SWIM keep per-node message load constant as the cluster grows?
options: By piggybacking membership updates on protocol pings and acks
By electing a coordinator that broadcasts membership
By heartbeating every member every second
quiz.why: Each node pings one random member per period and piggybacks updates, so load per node is constant and dissemination takes O(log N) rounds. All-to-all heartbeats grow O(N^2).

quiz.q: Why shard the real-time geo index by city then H3 parent cell rather than by driver_id hash?
options: Spatial queries then touch one or two shards instead of fanning out to all of them
Cell keys guarantee even load across shards
driver_id cannot be used as a Kafka key
quiz.why: Nearby queries are spatial; spatial keys keep them local. Cell keys do not give even load (geography is skewed) which is why hot cells need splitting.

quiz.q: Trip records are accessed mostly by trip_id. Which partitioning is best for the trip store inside a region?
quiz.why: Hashing on trip_id spreads load evenly and serves the dominant lookup. Partitioning by city makes a megacity one hot shard.

quiz.q: A Raft group has 5 replicas. How many simultaneous replica failures can it tolerate while still committing writes?
quiz.why: A majority of 3 out of 5 must remain, so 2 failures are tolerated. 3 is tempting but leaves only 2 nodes, not a majority.

quiz.q: In a Dynamo-style store with N=3, which setting guarantees read and write quorums overlap?
quiz.why: R + W > N means 2 + 2 = 4 > 3, so every read quorum intersects the latest write quorum. W=1, R=2 sums to 3, which is not greater than N.

quiz.q: Why is a quorum read/write (R + W > N) alone not enough to implement a safe driver reservation?
options: Overlap gives recency, but concurrent conditional writes need linearizable compare-and-set, which needs consensus or a single leader
Quorums only work with exactly 3 replicas
quiz.why: Two concurrent writers can both succeed against overlapping-but-different quorums; you need consensus for CAS. Speed is not the core problem.

quiz.q: Which PACELC classification best fits the payment ledger in this design?
quiz.why: Under partition the ledger refuses writes (C) and in normal operation pays coordination latency for consistency (C). PA/EL fits the location plane, not money.

quiz.q: During a network partition, the matcher can reach the geo index but not the driver lease store. What should happen?
options: Matching stalls and retries; nearby-cars display continues
Offer drivers anyway using the geo index state
Assign the driver and reconcile later
Fail over the whole region immediately
quiz.why: Assignment is CP by design: without the lease store we cannot guarantee single assignment. Assign-and-reconcile sounds pragmatic but produces two drivers driving to one rider.

quiz.q: Rider A arrives first: driver X is 1 min away, Y is 2 min. Rider B arrives 300 ms later: X is 1 min away, Y is 10 min. Total pickup minutes with greedy vs batched matching?
quiz.why: Greedy gives A the nearest (X), leaving B with Y: 1 + 10 = 11. Batched gives A Y and B X: 2 + 1 = 3. This is the canonical argument for batched assignment.

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of the Hungarian algorithm for an n x n assignment?
quiz.why: Hungarian (Kuhn-Munkres) runs in O(n^3), fine for hundreds per zone. O(n^2) is a common misremembering; exponential is brute force over permutations.

quiz.q: A zone has 5,000 requests and 10,000 drivers in one batch. What is the best approach?
options: Run full Hungarian on a dense 5,000 x 10,000 matrix
Increase the batch window to 60 s
Sparsify to top-K nearest drivers per request and solve with min-cost flow or an auction algorithm, possibly in subzones
quiz.why: Sparse graphs make the problem tractable; most far pairs are useless anyway. A dense O(n^3) solve is too slow and a 60 s window kills latency.

quiz.q: Why should dispatch rank candidates by road ETA rather than straight-line distance?
options: Straight-line distance is harder to compute
ETA is always shorter than distance
Rivers, one-way streets and highways can make a nearby driver many minutes away
quiz.why: Road topology dominates real pickup time. Haversine is cheaper, not harder, which is why it remains a fallback.

quiz.q: What is the main idea of contraction hierarchies?
options: Replace the road graph with a grid
Preprocess by contracting nodes in importance order and adding shortcuts, then query with an upward-only bidirectional search
quiz.why: Shortcuts preserve shortest paths, so queries settle only a few hundred nodes (~1 ms). Caching all pairs is quadratic in nodes and infeasible.

quiz.q: Plain contraction hierarchies have what weakness for live traffic?
options: Preprocessing assumes fixed weights, so changing weights requires costly re-preprocessing
They need A* heuristics to work
quiz.why: Customizable variants (CCH, CRP) separate topology from metrics so new traffic weights apply in seconds. CH returns exact shortest paths, so 'approximate' is wrong.

quiz.q: What makes A* faster than Dijkstra for point-to-point routing?
options: It only searches backward from the target
It uses an admissible heuristic (e.g. straight-line distance / max speed) to steer toward the target
quiz.why: An admissible heuristic never overestimates, so A* stays optimal while exploring fewer nodes. Shortcut edges are CH, not A*.

quiz.q: Uber's DeepETA model primarily does what?
options: Predicts the residual between the routing engine's ETA and actual arrival
quiz.why: DeepETA post-processes the routing ETA, learning its systematic error. Replacing routing would lose the physical model's generalisation.

quiz.q: Roughly how many ETA queries per second does dispatch need at 3,000 requests/s with 20 candidates each?
quiz.why: 3,000 x 20 = 60,000 per second, before quotes. This is why millisecond CH queries matter.

quiz.q: Surge is computed in 1-minute tumbling windows from mobile events that can arrive late. What mechanism decides when a window can be closed?
quiz.why: Watermarks estimate event-time progress; allowed lateness keeps windows open briefly for stragglers. Processing-time-only windows misattribute late mobile events.

quiz.q: Why does surge favour freshness and availability over consistency?
options: It is an estimate and the rider is protected by a signed upfront quote, so staleness or dropped late events are cheap
Surge data is legally required to be eventually consistent
quiz.why: The quote locks the price the rider sees, so what matters is timely signals. Flink can provide exactly-once state; it is a choice, not a limitation.

quiz.q: How does Uber run surge across regions according to its real-time infrastructure paper?
options: One region computes, others are idle
Each region computes only for its own cities and never fails over
Every region computes from aggregate Kafka, but a coordinator designates one primary region whose results are written
quiz.why: Active-active compute with a single writer gives fast failover because the standby's state is already warm. Idle standbys would need to rebuild large Flink state.

quiz.q: Which technique best prevents surge flicker between adjacent hexagons?
options: Spatial smoothing over kRing neighbours plus EWMA over time
quiz.why: Smoothing over neighbours and time removes sharp edges and jitter. Smaller cells make counts noisier and flicker worse.

quiz.q: Kafka offers exactly-once semantics. Why must the payments consumer still be idempotent?
options: Kafka EOS is disabled by default
Kafka EOS only covers consume-transform-produce within Kafka; a PSP call is an external side effect
Idempotency is only needed for ordering
quiz.why: A crash after charging but before committing the offset replays the message; only an idempotency key at the effect prevents a second charge. Defaults are irrelevant to the core issue.

quiz.q: What is the dual-write problem, and the standard fix?
options: Two services writing the same row; fix with sharding
Updating the DB and publishing an event separately can leave them inconsistent; fix with a transactional outbox or CDC
Writing to two replicas; fix with quorum
Two clients writing concurrently; fix with locks
quiz.why: A crash between the two writes loses an event or publishes a phantom one. Writing the event in the same transaction and relaying it fixes it.

quiz.q: Which idempotency key is best for the capture call on a completed trip?
options: A random UUID generated on each attempt
quiz.why: A deterministic natural key is reproduced by every retry from any service. A per-attempt UUID defeats idempotency; rider id would collide across trips.

quiz.q: Events for a trip must be consumed in order. What should the Kafka partition key be?
options: A random key for load balance
quiz.why: Kafka orders within a partition, so all of a trip's events must share a key. Random keys balance load but destroy per-trip order.

quiz.q: Why is 2PC a poor fit for trip + payment?
options: The PSP cannot participate in prepare/commit and 2PC blocks with locks if the coordinator fails
2PC cannot handle more than two services
quiz.why: External processors expose auth/capture/void, not prepare; 2PC also holds locks across slow calls. 2PC handles many participants, so the last option is wrong.

quiz.q: In the ride saga, what is the compensating action for an authorisation when the rider cancels before pickup?
quiz.why: Voiding releases the hold without moving money. Capture-then-refund moves money twice and costs fees; refund applies only after capture.

quiz.q: Why orchestrate the payment saga with a durable workflow engine (Cadence/Temporal) rather than pure event choreography?
options: A central, persisted workflow makes long multi-step money flows visible, retryable and resumable after crashes
Orchestration avoids the need for idempotency
quiz.why: Durable orchestration gives a single place to see and resume state. Steps still need idempotency because the engine retries.

quiz.q: A PSP capture call times out. What should the payments service do?
options: Mark PENDING and resolve by retrying or querying with the same idempotency key; reconcile later
Mark the trip unpaid and move on
Retry immediately with a new idempotency key
quiz.why: The charge may have succeeded; a new key could double charge. Charging a backup card without knowing the first outcome risks two charges.

quiz.q: In a double-entry ledger, a 20 unit fare (18 to driver, 2 platform fee) produces entries that must sum to what?
quiz.why: Double entry means every order's entries sum to zero: -20 rider escrow, +18 driver, +2 platform. Uber's Gulfstream describes this model; any non-zero sum signals a bug.

quiz.q: Why do drivers' apps use a persistent WebSocket/MQTT connection for offers instead of relying on FCM/APNs?
options: WebSockets are encrypted, push is not
Platform push is best-effort with no latency guarantee, and offers expire in about 15 s
quiz.why: The offer window is short; OS push can be delayed or throttled. Push is still used as a fallback to wake backgrounded apps.

quiz.q: A notification service must push a message to rider R. How does it know which gateway node holds R's connection?
options: DNS lookup of the rider's IP
A connection registry mapping user -> gateway node with TTL
quiz.why: A registry routes server-initiated messages precisely. Broadcasting to hundreds of gateways for every message wastes bandwidth.

quiz.q: Which protocol property makes MQTT attractive for drivers on flaky 2G/3G networks?
options: It guarantees exactly-once end-to-end to the database
It is the only protocol supporting TLS
Small headers, keepalives, QoS levels and session resumption
quiz.why: MQTT was designed for constrained, unreliable links. Its QoS 2 is exactly-once between client and broker only, not end-to-end to downstream systems.

quiz.q: 8 million concurrent connections at 50,000 per gateway node need roughly how many nodes before headroom?
quiz.why: 8,000,000 / 50,000 = 160. Production runs more for zone failure and deploy headroom.

quiz.q: A gateway node with 50,000 connections dies. What prevents a reconnect storm from overloading the remaining nodes?
options: Clients reconnect immediately in a tight loop
Exponential backoff with full jitter on the client plus admission control on gateways
quiz.why: Jitter spreads reconnects over time; token-bucket admission sheds the rest with Retry-After. Tight loops create a thundering herd.

quiz.q: What does a fixed-window rate limiter allow that a token bucket or sliding window prevents?
options: A burst of up to twice the limit around a window boundary
quiz.why: With 100/min, 100 at 0:59 and 100 at 1:00 is 200 in seconds. Token buckets bound bursts by bucket size.

quiz.q: Why rate limit driver pings when the company controls the driver app?
options: Buggy releases, modified clients and spoofing tools can flood the ingest path
quiz.why: A bad client release multiplying ping rate would overload shared shards; limits contain it and flag abnormal devices.

quiz.q: Matcher A reserves a driver with a 15 s lease, then pauses for 20 s in garbage collection. Matcher B reserves the same driver. What prevents A from overwriting B when it wakes?
options: A's lease is still valid locally
Ringpop forwards A's write to B
Fencing token: the store rejects A's write with an older token
quiz.why: Monotonic fencing tokens let the storage reject stale holders regardless of their local belief. Clocks cannot guarantee mutual exclusion.

quiz.q: Why is a single-instance Redis SETNX lock unsafe for preventing double assignment?
options: Failover to an async replica can lose the lock, and a paused client can outlive its TTL
quiz.why: Async replication and process pauses both break mutual exclusion. Such locks are fine for efficiency, not correctness. SET with NX and PX does support expiry.

quiz.q: Where in this design is leader election (single writer) appropriate?
options: For the surge output writer and each outbox relay partition
quiz.why: One writer avoids conflicting multipliers and duplicate relays. Electing leaders on the ping path would bottleneck 1.25M writes/s.

quiz.q: A whole region hosting Bengaluru fails. What is the fastest way to restore the live driver index in the standby region?
options: Restore it from last night's backup
Let drivers' next pings rebuild it within one ping interval
Ask drivers to log in again
quiz.why: Soft state regenerates for free from pings in about 4 s. Synchronous replication of 1.25M writes/s across regions would be expensive and unnecessary.

quiz.q: Uber described storing what on the driver's phone to survive datacenter failover?
options: An encrypted digest of trip state
quiz.why: Dispatch periodically sends an encrypted state digest; after failover, an unknown trip is restored from it, avoiding synchronous cross-region trip replication.

quiz.q: Why home each city in one region rather than letting all regions accept writes for any trip?
options: It reduces the number of regions needed
Cities cannot be served from more than one region by law
It avoids conflicting concurrent transitions on the same trip that cannot be merged
quiz.why: Per-partition homing gives active-active capacity without write conflicts. Data residency applies to some countries, not universally.

quiz.q: With three regions and N+1 failover capacity, roughly what peak utilisation should each region run at normally?
quiz.why: If one fails, the other two absorb its load: 1.5x their normal load must stay under about 80-90%, so roughly 55-60% each. Running at 80% means failover causes a second outage.

quiz.q: Rider cancel and driver start arrive simultaneously at the trip service. With optimistic concurrency, what happens?
options: Both succeed and the trip is both CANCELLED and ON_TRIP
The first conditional update wins; the second gets a version conflict (409) with the current state
The later timestamp wins regardless of order
quiz.why: Version checks serialise transitions without locks. Timestamp-wins is last-writer-wins, which silently discards a valid transition.

quiz.q: The trip state store is Docstore-like. What gives it strict serializability per partition?
options: Raft consensus with a single leader per partition over MySQL
quiz.why: Each partition is a Raft group; writes go through the leader and commit on quorum. Gossip is eventual and gives no ordering guarantees.

quiz.q: Schemaless stores data as immutable cells keyed by row key, column name and ref key. How is an update represented?
options: Append a new cell with a higher ref key; the highest ref key is current
Store a diff in a separate table
quiz.why: Append-only versions make cells a change log that triggers can follow. In-place overwrite is exactly what Schemaless avoids.

quiz.q: GPS in an urban canyon puts a driver on a parallel street. Which technique best corrects the trail used for fares?
options: Map matching (e.g. HMM over road segments) using heading and speed
quiz.why: Map matching snaps noisy points to the most likely road path. Averaging smears across streets and the rider's phone has the same urban canyon problem.

quiz.q: An older ping arrives after a newer one for the same driver. How should the location service handle it?
options: Apply it, since all pings are valid
Average it with the newer position
Drop it because its sequence number is not greater than the last accepted
Store it and re-sort the index
quiz.why: Per-driver sequence numbers make updates monotonic so the driver never jumps backwards. Averaging introduces a fake position.

quiz.q: A ride request is retried by the app after a timeout, with the same Idempotency-Key. What should POST /trips return?
options: The original 201 response for the existing trip
quiz.why: Insert-if-absent on (rider_id, key) returns the stored result. Always 409 forces clients to treat success as failure.

quiz.q: Where should the payment authorisation happen in the ride flow?
options: At request time, before or alongside matching
quiz.why: Authorising at request confirms funds before a driver drives to the rider; capture comes after. Authorising only at completion risks unpaid trips.

quiz.q: The surge Flink job crashes and stops writing. What should the quote API do?
options: Return errors until the job recovers
Set every cell to maximum surge
Use last known multipliers decaying toward 1.0x, capped, while the standby writer is promoted
quiz.why: Graceful degradation keeps rides flowing. Per-quote recomputation would hammer stores and still lack the windowed state.

quiz.q: Which failure is the design deliberately willing to turn into unavailability rather than inconsistency?
options: Driver assignment when the lease store is unreachable
quiz.why: Assignment is CP: no lease, no offer. The others degrade with stale or approximate data.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of a cell-based architecture for this system?
options: It removes the need for databases
Failures, bad deploys and overload stay contained to the cities served by one cell
quiz.why: Cells limit blast radius and allow staged deploys. They do not change consistency guarantees or prevent partitions.

quiz.q: The ETA service is overloaded during a spike. Which degradation order is best?
options: Prioritise dispatch ETAs; degrade quote ETAs to cached tables, then haversine x city factor
Turn off matching to save ETA capacity
quiz.why: Dispatch ETAs directly create trips; quote and display ETAs can be approximate. Shedding dispatch first breaks the core flow.

quiz.q: Roughly how much trip-row storage per day for 25M trips at 5 KB each, before replication?
quiz.why: 25,000,000 x 5 KB = 125 GB/day, ~45 TB/year before 3x replication. Trails are separate and larger.

quiz.q: Why are multipliers written to the KV store with a TTL of a few minutes?
options: So that if the writer stops, stale surge expires and the fallback path kicks in instead of serving old prices indefinitely
quiz.why: TTL bounds staleness; readers detect missing entries and use a safe fallback. Memory is trivial here.

quiz.q: Which signal would most directly reveal a double-assignment bug in production?
options: Count of drivers with more than one active trip
quiz.why: An invariant check (must be 0) catches the bug directly. The others are health signals that would not isolate it.

quiz.q: When is batched matching NOT worth its extra latency?
options: In dense downtown zones at rush hour
In sparse areas where requests rarely compete for the same drivers
quiz.why: Batching helps only when requests compete; in sparse areas greedy gives the same result faster. The other three are exactly where batching pays off.
